topics.title: Accounting rate of return
topics.summary: The first of the five decision rules compares average accounting profit with the average book value of the money tied up. It is easy to compute but uses accounting numbers, not cash flows, and ignores the time value of money. Know the formula and why it can only be a relative comparison.

topics.title: Payback
topics.summary: Payback asks how many years it takes to get the initial investment back; discounted payback asks the same after discounting each flow. Both are quick screens that ignore everything after the recovery date. Practise the cumulative table and the fractional year.

topics.title: Net present value
topics.summary: NPV = CF0 + PV is the rule that tracks shareholder wealth, so it wins whenever rules conflict. The four-step sequence organizes the analysis from cash flows to the accept/reject decision.

topics.title: Internal rate of return
topics.summary: IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV zero, the project's own return. It matches NPV for conventional flows, but fails with several sign changes, with financing-type flows, and when ranking mutually exclusive projects. The NPV profile and crossover rate show why.

topics.title: Profitability index
topics.summary: The PI divides the PV of the inflows by the PV of the outflows, a benefit/cost ratio. It gives the same accept/reject answer as NPV but a different ranking, because it measures profit per dollar invested.

topics.title: Project relationships and rationing
topics.summary: Projects can be independent, dependent or mutually exclusive, and that decides how the decision rules are used. When funds run out, positive-NPV projects must be rejected (capital rationing) and the PI ranks them.

topics.title: Unequal lives
topics.summary: Mutually exclusive projects with different lives cannot be compared on raw NPV. Convert them with the equivalent annual value (EAV), a constant chain of replacement (CCR, NPV to infinity) or the lowest common multiple of the lives.

concepts.definition: ARR (ROC) = expected average annual profit after tax divided by average investment, where average investment = (I0 + book value at the end of the project)/2. ROE and ROA use average book equity and average assets as the denominator instead.
concepts.explain: ARR compares accounting profit with the average book value of the capital tied up in the project. It is quick to calculate, but it uses accounting figures (which may include accruals) rather than cash flows, ignores the time value of money and averages a multi-year project into one number. It is a relative comparison against the ROC of your other projects or a target, never an absolute decision on its own.
concepts.example: A project costs $900,000 and will have a book value of $300,000 at the end. Average profit after tax is $90,000 a year. Average investment = (900,000 + 300,000)/2 = $600,000, so ARR = 90,000/600,000 = 15.00%. Sample exam Q10(a): $215,000 / [($1.2M + $0.96M)/2] = 19.91% per annum.
concepts.contrast: ARR is a ratio of accounting numbers (profit over book value) with no discounting; IRR is the discount rate that sets the NPV of the cash flows to zero. ARR is not payback (a time in years) and not a cash yield (profit, not cash flow, over the average rather than the initial investment). ROC, ROE and ROA differ only in the denominator.
concepts.trap: Dividing by I0 instead of the average investment (arr-divide-i0); using cash flow instead of profit after tax (arr-cash-not-profit); comparing ARR with the discount rate R and calling it an accept decision. Cue words: "net income", "residual value", "average", "state the decision" (answer: relative only; use NPV).
concepts.mnemonic: Average profit over average investment: two averages.
concepts.formula: ARR = avg annual profit after tax / [(I0 + book value at end)/2]

concepts.definition: The payback period is the time, in years and part years, until the cumulative undiscounted cash flows equal the initial investment. Accept the project if its payback is shorter than a preset limit.
concepts.explain: Cumulate the cash flows year by year, find the year in which the investment is recovered, and add the fraction of that year: amount still to recover divided by that year's cash flow. The maths is easy and quick, but payback ignores the time value of money, ignores all income after the payback date (so it is biased against long projects) and needs an arbitrary cutoff. It is a relative comparison only.
concepts.example: Cost $120,000; cash flows $30,000, $40,000, $45,000, $50,000. Cumulative: 30,000; 70,000; 115,000. After year 3, $5,000 remains and year 4 brings $50,000: 5,000/50,000 = 0.1, so payback = 3.1 years. For level flows, payback = cost / annual flow (for example $1,370,000 / $285,000 = 4.81 years).
concepts.contrast: Payback adds raw cash flows; discounted payback adds present values at R. A payback shorter than the life guarantees NPV > 0 only at a zero discount rate. Payback measures liquidity (time to get cash back), not value created.
concepts.trap: Counting the whole recovery year (payback-after-recovery: 4.00 instead of 3.1); dividing the remainder by the previous year's flow; applying the cost/annual-flow shortcut to uneven flows or beyond the life (if the total inflow never reaches the cost, the project never pays back).
concepts.mnemonic: Years before recovery + remaining over next.
concepts.formula: Payback = k + (I0 - cumulative CF_k) / CF_(k+1);  level flows: I0 / CF

concepts.definition: The discounted payback period is the time until the cumulative present values of the cash flows, CF_t/(1+R)^t, equal the initial investment.
concepts.explain: It is the payback table with each flow discounted at R first, so it removes the time-value criticism. It still ignores income after the discounted payback date and still needs a cutoff. For conventional flows and R > 0 it is always longer than the ordinary payback, and if it is shorter than the project's life, the NPV is positive.
concepts.example: Cost 100; four flows of 40; R = 10%. Ordinary payback = 2.5 years. PVs: 36.36, 33.06, 30.05, 27.32; cumulative PV after year 3 = 99.47, so 0.53 remains: 0.53/27.32 = 0.02. Discounted payback = 3.02 years (SM 9-4 style).
concepts.contrast: Payback vs discounted payback: raw flows vs present values. Discounted payback < life implies NPV > 0; ordinary payback < life implies nothing at R > 0. Both ignore flows after the recovery date and give only a relative comparison.
concepts.trap: Dividing the PV remainder by the undiscounted flow of the recovery year (both parts must be in PV terms); accumulating undiscounted flows by mistake; forgetting that a project can pay back in raw terms yet never in PV terms (the project then has NPV < 0).
concepts.formula: accumulate CF_t/(1+R)^t until = I0;  fraction = PV still to recover / PV of next flow

concepts.definition: NPV = CF0 + PV, where PV = CF1/(1+R) + CF2/(1+R)^2 + ... and CF0 is negative (the initial outlay), so NPV = PV of future cash flows - initial investment. Accept the project if NPV > 0.
concepts.explain: NPV is the expected change in shareholder wealth, in today's dollars, after the time value of money. It gives an absolute accept/reject decision on each project as well as a relative comparison, and it is the rule that serves shareholders, so when another rule disagrees, NPV wins. Its one weakness is that it ignores the amount of capital tied up (the PI deals with that).
concepts.contrast: NPV is a dollar amount at the required return R; IRR is a percentage you compare with R; PI is a ratio. Excel's NPV() is really a PV() and discounts the first value by one period: add the outlay separately.
concepts.trap: Entering CF0 with the wrong sign (sign-cf0); treating the outlay as year 1 (cf0-as-period-1); forgetting to add the residual (dropped-salvage-term) or not discounting it (salvage-not-discounted); reporting the PV of the inflows as the NPV. NPV = 0 means indifferent; negative NPV projects are sometimes forced (environmental repair).
concepts.mnemonic: NPV = what it is worth (PV) minus what it costs (CF0).

concepts.definition: The professor's sequence: (1) work out the expected after-tax cash flows CF0, CF1, ...; (2) decide the discount rate and discount to today; (3) if lives are unequal, equalize them with EAV or CCR; (4) decide: independent projects, accept if NPV > 0; mutually exclusive projects, accept the highest positive NPV (the least negative if you must take one).
concepts.explain: Steps 1 and 2 are the hard parts (forecasting incremental after-tax cash flows and choosing R). Step 3 only matters when mutually exclusive projects have different lives. Step 4 is the decision: each independent project is judged on NPV > 0, while mutually exclusive projects compete and only the best NPV survives.
concepts.example: Projects P and Q (3-year lives, R = 10%) have NPV(P) = +$15,154.02 and NPV(Q) = +$14,522.92. Same lives, so skip step 3; both positive but mutually exclusive, so accept P (the higher NPV), even though Q has the higher IRR.
concepts.contrast: Independent vs mutually exclusive in step 4: independent means accept all with NPV > 0; mutually exclusive means accept only the best. Step 3 (equalize lives) is different from step 2 (discount to today).
concepts.trap: Skipping step 3 when lives differ and comparing raw NPVs; rejecting a forced project because its NPV is negative; using IRR or PI to pick between mutually exclusive projects.

concepts.definition: The IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV = 0: 0 = CF0 + CF1/(1+IRR) + ... + CFN/(1+IRR)^N. For conventional cash flows, accept if IRR > R and reject if IRR < R.
concepts.explain: IRR is what the project returns; R is the return you need. It is the same idea as the yield to maturity on a bond. For conventional flows (CF0 negative, all later flows positive or zero) the NPV profile crosses zero once, so IRR > R means NPV > 0 and the two rules agree. It uses the time value of money and shows the size of the return, but it can have several answers when the flows change sign.
concepts.example: Flows -1,000, +600, +600: x = 1/(1+IRR) solves 600x^2 + 600x - 1,000 = 0, so IRR = 13.07%. With R = 10%, IRR > R: accept (NPV at 10% = +41.32). With R = 15%, IRR < R: reject. Closed forms: single payment IRR = (FV/PV)^(1/N) - 1; level perpetuity IRR = CF/cost.
concepts.contrast: IRR vs R: the project's own return vs the return required. IRR vs ARR: discount rate vs accounting ratio. IRR vs YTM: the same calculation applied to a project instead of a bond. The IRR rule is a shortcut for NPV only when flows are conventional.
concepts.trap: Comparing the wrong way round (irr-direction: accepting when IRR < R); using the rule with unconventional or financing-type flows; computing IRR as average gain per year (no compounding); choosing the higher IRR among mutually exclusive projects.
concepts.mnemonic: IRR above R: go. IRR below R: no.
concepts.formula: NPV(IRR) = 0;  accept if IRR > R (conventional flows)

concepts.definition: An NPV profile is the graph of a project's NPV against the discount rate. Its vertical intercept (R = 0) is the sum of the undiscounted cash flows, it approaches CF0 as R grows without limit, and it crosses the horizontal axis at the IRR(s).
concepts.explain: For conventional flows the profile slopes downward because a higher R shrinks the PV of the later inflows while the outlay at t = 0 stays put. Reading it: left of the IRR NPV is positive (accept), right of the IRR it is negative (reject). For financing-type flows it slopes upward, and unconventional flows can make it cross the axis more than once.
concepts.example: Flows -1,000, +600, +600: NPV(0%) = +200 (the sum), NPV(10%) = +41.32, NPV(20%) = -83.33, and it crosses zero at the IRR = 13.07%. As R becomes very large, NPV tends to -1,000.
concepts.contrast: NPV profile vs payback or cash-flow timeline (a profile has the discount rate on the horizontal axis). Conventional (downward) vs financing-type (upward) profiles. The IRR is read at the crossing; the required return is where you read your own NPV.
concepts.trap: Thinking NPV approaches zero for very high R (it approaches CF0); forgetting that NPV at 0% is just the sum of the flows including the outlay; assuming every profile slopes downward.
concepts.mnemonic: Left of the IRR positive, right of it negative.
concepts.formula: NPV(R = 0) = sum of CF_t;  NPV(R -> infinity) -> CF0

concepts.definition: A project can have as many IRRs as there are sign changes in its cash flows (a rule-of-signs upper limit). With unconventional flows there may be several IRRs, or none, so the rule "accept if IRR > R" is not reliable and the NPV at R must decide.
concepts.explain: Solving NPV = 0 means finding the roots of an equation, and a profile that crosses the axis several times has several roots. Unconventional flows arise from big maintenance or clean-up costs late in the life and from incremental (A minus B) streams. A calculator shows just one root, so check the NPV at R or the profile.
concepts.example: Flows -500,000; +1,235,000; -756,000 have two IRRs, 12% and 35%. NPV is positive only between them: NPV(25%) = +4,160.00 (accept) but NPV(8%) = -4,629.63 even though both IRRs exceed 8%. The flows -500,000; +800,000; -400,000 have no real IRR at all (discriminant < 0).
concepts.contrast: Conventional (one sign change, at most one IRR) vs unconventional (several sign changes). Multiple IRRs (several rates give NPV = 0) vs financing-type flows (one IRR but the rule reverses).
concepts.trap: Trusting the single IRR the calculator returns; accepting because "both IRRs exceed R"; believing two sign changes always give exactly two IRRs. When NPV and IRR disagree, use NPV (seminar 5).
concepts.mnemonic: Count the sign flips: that many IRRs, at most.
concepts.formula: max number of IRRs = number of sign changes in CF0, CF1, ..., CFN

concepts.definition: Financing-type flows have a cash inflow first and outflows later (CF0 positive, later flows negative). The IRR is then a rate you pay, not earn, and the rule reverses: accept only if IRR < R.
concepts.explain: Think of borrowing: you receive money now and repay later. The NPV profile slopes upward, so NPV rises with R. Customer prepayments before the work is done are an example. The NPV at R gives the right decision and avoids the sign confusion.
concepts.example: Receive $200 now and pay $236 in a year: IRR = 236/200 - 1 = 18%. At R = 12% the NPV is 200 - 236/1.12 = -$10.71, so reject: the money costs 18%, more than the 12% you can earn elsewhere. Accept only if R > 18%.
concepts.contrast: Investing-type flows (outlay first): accept if IRR > R, downward profile. Financing-type flows (inflow first): accept if IRR < R, upward profile. Both give a single IRR; unlike multiple IRRs, the problem here is the direction of the rule.
concepts.trap: Applying the standard rule (IRR > R) and accepting a costly source of funds; reading the NPV profile slope backwards (irr-direction).
concepts.mnemonic: Money in first means you are the borrower: low IRR wins.

concepts.term: Ranking conflict between NPV and IRR
concepts.definition: For mutually exclusive projects, NPV and IRR can rank the projects differently because of scale (different outlays) or timing (different patterns of flows). The correct choice is the higher NPV at the required return R, equivalently the incremental IRR (A minus B, with A the bigger project) beating R.
concepts.explain: Only one project can be taken, so the question is which adds more wealth, and that is the NPV. A smaller project can have a higher IRR but a lower NPV. Two ways to settle it: compute both NPVs at R, or compute the IRR of the difference in cash flows and compare it with R.
concepts.contrast: Independent projects: IRR and NPV agree for conventional flows. Mutually exclusive projects: they can disagree, and NPV is right. The crossover rate tells where the NPV ranking flips.
concepts.trap: Picking the higher IRR (picked-higher-irr); comparing PI ranks across different scales; forgetting that the ranking can depend on R (it changes at the crossover rate).
concepts.mnemonic: Pick the bigger wealth, not the bigger percentage.
concepts.formula: choose max NPV at R;  or accept A over B if IRR(A - B) > R

concepts.definition: The crossover rate is the discount rate at which two projects have equal NPV; it is the IRR of the difference in their cash flows (A minus B, subtracting year by year including CF0). Below it the project with the higher NPV at low rates wins; above it the other wins.
concepts.explain: Subtract the two cash-flow lists year by year; the IRR of that incremental stream is the crossover rate. It does not matter which project you subtract from which, but the ranges must be stated carefully: compare R with the crossover to see which project is better.
concepts.contrast: Crossover rate (where NPVs are equal, IRR of A - B) vs each project's own IRR (where its own NPV is zero). The difference of two conventional streams can be unconventional, so check for multiple crossovers.
concepts.trap: Mis-stating which project wins below or above the crossover; subtracting in different years; confusing the crossover with an IRR of one project; PI ranking on different scales.
concepts.mnemonic: Equal NPV where the difference has zero NPV.
concepts.formula: Crossover = IRR of (A - B) cash flows

concepts.definition: The MIRR modifies the cash flows first (discounting outflows, compounding inflows at the required return, or a combination) so that only one sign change remains, then computes an IRR on the two modified flows.
concepts.explain: MIRR was proposed to remove the multiple-IRR problem. It is controversial: there are several different MIRRs, it is not a true rate of return, and you must already know the required return, in which case the NPV answers the question directly. Low priority for the exam; know the idea.
concepts.example: Flows -1,000; +600; +700 at R = 10%. Reinvestment approach: FV of inflows at the end = 600 x 1.10 + 700 = 1,360; MIRR = (1,360/1,000)^(1/2) - 1 = 16.62%, below the IRR of 18.88% because the 600 is reinvested at 10%, not at the IRR.
concepts.contrast: MIRR (modified flows, one answer) vs IRR (the actual flows, possibly several answers). MIRR is not the same as the required return.
concepts.trap: Calling the MIRR a true rate of return; forgetting that different MIRR methods give different numbers; thinking IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR (the NPV and IRR are not affected by what is done with the cash).
concepts.formula: MIRR = (FV of inflows at R / PV of outflows at R)^(1/N) - 1

concepts.definition: PI = PV of cash inflows / PV of cash outflows. For conventional flows PI = PV / initial outlay = 1 + NPV/outlay. Accept if PI > 1 (NPV > 0); reject if PI < 1.
concepts.explain: The PI is bang for the buck: the present value you get for each dollar you put in. Its accept/reject decision always matches the NPV, but it ranks by profitability per dollar, which is what matters when capital is limited. A PI of 0.98 means the project is rejected; the PI is 1-based, not 0-based.
concepts.example: Using the NPV example above: PV of inflows = 11,516.69 and outlay = 10,000, so PI = 1.1517 (= 1 + 1,516.69/10,000). PI > 1: accept. A project with PV of inflows $38,200 and outlay $40,000 has PI = 0.955: reject.
concepts.contrast: PI (PV/outlay, 1-based) vs the alternative 0-based version NPV/outlay: adding or subtracting 1 gives the same rankings. PI vs NPV: same decision, different ranking.
concepts.trap: Reading a PI below 1 as acceptable (PI = 0.98 is a reject); using NPV/outlay and calling it PI > 1 (pi-zero-based); using PI to choose between mutually exclusive projects of different scale.
concepts.mnemonic: PI above one: you get back more than you put in.
concepts.formula: PI = PV of inflows / PV of outflows = 1 + NPV / initial outlay

concepts.term: PI versus NPV: the same decision, different ranking
concepts.definition: NPV and PI always give the same accept/reject decision for a single project, but they can rank projects differently: NPV ranks on the dollar change in wealth and ignores capital tied up, while PI ranks on profit per dollar of capital.
concepts.explain: A big project can have the larger NPV and the smaller PI. For mutually exclusive projects of different scale, use the NPV (it measures wealth). Under capital rationing, use the PI (it ranks the best use of each scarce dollar).
concepts.example: Mutually exclusive S (outlay 40,000, PV 52,000: NPV 12,000, PI 1.30) and L (outlay 150,000, PV 175,000: NPV 25,000, PI 1.17). NPV picks L; PI picks S. If both could be done with enough funds, accept both (both NPV > 0).
concepts.contrast: Which is best: NPV (mutually exclusive, no budget limit) vs PI (independent projects under a budget limit). PI and NPV both accept at PI > 1 / NPV > 0.
concepts.trap: Using PI to rank mutually exclusive projects that differ in scale (the SM 9-16 trap); using NPV to rank projects when funds are limited; mixing the 1-based and 0-based PI when comparing.
concepts.mnemonic: NPV measures size; PI measures efficiency.

concepts.term: Independent, dependent and mutually exclusive projects
concepts.definition: Independent projects can be taken in any combination without affecting each other's values; dependent projects affect each other's values (one makes the other worth more or less); mutually exclusive projects can only be taken one at a time, which includes timing and replacement decisions.
concepts.explain: The relationship decides how the rules are used. Independent: accept each with NPV > 0. Mutually exclusive: pick the best, equalizing lives if needed. Timing decisions (when to replace, retire or close) are mutually exclusive: pick the timing with the maximum NPV.
concepts.example: A new delivery van and a new website are independent. A new restaurant whose customers depend on a new highway exit is dependent on that exit. Machine A versus Machine B for the same job are mutually exclusive, and so are "replace now" versus "replace in two years".
concepts.contrast: Independent (no effect on each other) vs dependent (one changes the other's cash flows) vs mutually exclusive (taking one rules out the others). Mutually exclusive projects are chosen by NPV, not by accepting everything positive.
concepts.trap: Treating mutually exclusive projects as independent and accepting both; forgetting that timing and replacement decisions are mutually exclusive choices.
concepts.mnemonic: Independent: all that pass. Exclusive: only the best.

concepts.definition: Capital rationing is rejecting positive-NPV projects because of a lack of funds (or people). When projects are independent, rank them by PI and take them in rank order until the budget is used.
concepts.explain: Without a budget limit, every independent project with NPV > 0 is accepted. With a hard limit the firm must choose, and the best choice maximizes total NPV per dollar spent, so rank by PI. It is a soft constraint when set internally and a hard one when the capital market denies funds.
concepts.example: Budget $400,000. B (outlay 200,000, NPV 50,000, PI 1.25), D (100,000, NPV 18,000, PI 1.18), E (100,000, NPV 14,000, PI 1.14), A (300,000, NPV 36,000, PI 1.12). Rank by PI: B, D, E use $400,000 for total NPV $82,000; A is rejected despite its positive NPV. Sample exam Q5: capital rationing = "rejecting a positive NPV project because of a lack of funds".
concepts.contrast: Capital rationing (a funds constraint on independent projects, rank by PI) vs mutually exclusive choices (rank by NPV) vs simply stopping to analyse projects in bad markets (not rationing).
concepts.trap: Ranking by NPV or by IRR when funds are limited; calling a pause in project analysis "rationing"; forgetting the best set of projects can leave some budget unused.
concepts.formula: rank by PI = PV inflows / outlay, take in order until the budget is gone

concepts.term: Equivalent annual value (EAV / EAA / EAB / EAC)
concepts.definition: The equivalent annual value converts an NPV into the level annual amount over the project's life with the same present value: EAV = NPV / annuity factor(R, N), with annuity factor = [1 - (1+R)^-N]/R. For costs it is the equivalent annual cost (EAC).
concepts.explain: Use it to compare mutually exclusive projects with unequal lives that will be repeated: compare the annual amounts, not the raw NPVs. Higher EAV (or lower EAC) wins. The annuity factor comes from the table sheet or the formula, using each project's own life N.
concepts.example: Two maintenance programs at R = 10%: spend $2.0M for 2 years of work, or $2.7M for 3 years. Annuity factors: 1.7355 and 2.4869. EAC = 2.0/1.7355 = $1.1524M a year versus 2.7/2.4869 = $1.0857M a year. The 3-year program is cheaper per year.
concepts.contrast: EAV (annual amount) vs CCR (NPV to infinity) vs LCM (repeat to a common horizon): all give the same ranking. EAV = NPV / annuity factor; CCR = EAV / R.
concepts.trap: Comparing raw NPVs of unequal-life projects (raw-npv-unequal-lives); using the wrong N in the annuity factor (wrong-n-annuity); sign confusion with costs (smaller cost wins).
concepts.mnemonic: Spread the NPV over the years: NPV over the annuity factor.

concepts.term: Constant chain of replacement and lowest common multiple
concepts.definition: CCR (NPV to infinity) values the project replaced forever: CCR = NPV x (1+R)^N / ((1+R)^N - 1) = EAV/R. The lowest common multiple (LCM) method repeats each project until the lives meet, repeating the whole NPV at each replacement.
concepts.explain: These are two other ways to put unequal lives on the same footing. The LCM horizon for lives of 2 and 3 years is 6 years: repeat the 2-year program three times and the 3-year program twice. All three methods (EAV, CCR, LCM) rank the projects identically.
concepts.example: Programs of $2.0M for 2 years and $2.7M for 3 years at 10%: CCR = -2.0 x 1.21/0.21 = -$11.5238M versus -2.7 x 1.331/0.331 = -$10.8571M. LCM over 6 years: -$5.0189M versus -$4.7285M; scaling by 1.1^6/(1.1^6 - 1) gives the same CCRs. The two programs have equal annual cost at 26.27% per annum.
concepts.contrast: CCR is EAV capitalized as a perpetuity (EAV / R); LCM stops at a common horizon. Do not compare raw NPVs or stop at the shorter life.
concepts.trap: Repeating only the cost and not the whole NPV in the LCM method; applying (1+R)^N with the wrong N; comparing signs the wrong way for costs (the less negative CCR wins).
concepts.mnemonic: Chain the project forever: EAV over R.

activities.title: Order the four NPV steps
activities.prompt: Put the professor's four-step NPV analysis in the correct order.
items: Work out the expected after-tax cash flows CF0, CF1, CF2, ...
Decide the discount rate and discount the cash flows back to today
If projects have unequal lives, make them equivalent with EAV or CCR
Decide: accept NPV > 0 (independent) or the highest NPV (mutually exclusive)
activities.explanation: You cannot discount before you have the cash flows, you cannot compare unequal lives before you have NPVs, and the accept/reject decision comes last.

activities.prompt: Sort each statement under the decision rule it describes.

activities.explanation: ARR and payback are accounting/relative rules; NPV tracks shareholder wealth and ignores capital tied up; IRR is the project's own return and breaks down for unconventional flows.

activities.title: Match the rule to its decision criterion
activities.prompt: Match each decision rule to the condition under which it says accept.

pairs.right: Compares favourably with the ROC of other projects or a target (relative only)
Shorter than a preset limit in years
Present values recover the cost sooner than the preset limit
Greater than R, for conventional cash flows

activities.explanation: Only NPV, IRR and PI give an absolute decision against a market benchmark; ARR and the payback rules are relative comparisons against internal limits.

activities.title: Order the payback steps
activities.prompt: Put the steps for calculating a payback period with uneven cash flows in order.
items: Write the cumulative cash flows year by year
Find the year in which the cumulative total first covers the initial investment
Divide the amount still unrecovered at the start of that year by that year's cash flow
Add the fraction to the number of whole years completed before that year
activities.explanation: Payback = whole years before recovery + (remaining / next year's flow). Reversing the divisor to the previous year's flow is a classic slip.

activities.title: Accept or reject?
activities.prompt: Sort each result into the decision it implies (conventional cash flows, firm's required return as stated).

items.text: IRR = 14% with R = 11%
Discounted payback 3.4 years on a 5-year life
IRR = 9% with R = 12%
Payback 4.2 years against a 3-year limit

activities.explanation: Accept on NPV > 0, PI > 1, IRR > R (conventional flows), or a discounted payback inside the life. A payback longer than the preset limit fails the payback screen.

activities.title: Cash-flow pattern and its IRR problem
activities.prompt: Match each cash-flow pattern to what it implies for the IRR.

pairs.right: At most one IRR; IRR > R agrees with NPV > 0
Up to two IRRs; NPV at R decides
Financing type: accept only if IRR < R
No real IRR; NPV is negative at every rate

activities.explanation: The number of IRRs is limited by the sign changes; whenever the pattern is not conventional, rely on the NPV at the required return.

formulas.name: Net present value
formulas.when: Every discounted-cash-flow decision: CF0 is the (negative) outlay at t = 0 and the rest is the PV of the inflows.
formulas.trap: CF0 is negative and is not discounted; Excel's NPV() is a PV() that discounts the first value one period.

formulas.name: Profitability index
formulas.formula: PI = PV of inflows / PV of outflows = 1 + NPV / outlay
formulas.when: To rank independent projects under capital rationing; accept if PI > 1.
formulas.trap: It is 1-based (PI 0.98 is a reject); NPV/outlay is the 0-based variant, and PI can mis-rank mutually exclusive projects of different scale.

formulas.name: Internal rate of return
formulas.when: Find the project's own return with the calculator CF worksheet; accept if IRR > R for conventional flows.
formulas.trap: Multiple IRRs with sign changes and a reversed rule for financing-type flows; the calculator shows just one root.

formulas.name: Crossover rate
formulas.formula: Crossover = IRR of the difference in cash flows (A - B)
formulas.when: Mutually exclusive projects whose NPV ranking changes with R.
formulas.trap: Subtract year by year including CF0; then state which project wins below and above the crossover.

formulas.name: Payback period
formulas.formula: Payback = years before recovery + (amount still to recover) / (next year's cash flow)
formulas.when: A quick screen of how fast the investment is recovered; accept if shorter than a preset limit.
formulas.trap: Do not count the whole recovery year or divide by the previous year's flow; if the total inflow is below the cost, the project never pays back.

formulas.name: Discounted payback
formulas.formula: accumulate CF_t/(1+R)^t until the total equals I0; fraction = PV still to recover / PV of next flow
formulas.when: The payback screen with the time value of money included.
formulas.trap: Both the numerator and the denominator of the fraction must be present values.

formulas.name: Accounting rate of return (ROC)
formulas.formula: ARR = average annual profit after tax / [(I0 + book value at end)/2]
formulas.when: Accounting screen comparing a project's return on capital with other projects.
formulas.trap: Use profit, not cash flow, and divide by the average investment, not I0; do not compare with the discount rate.

formulas.name: Equivalent annual value
formulas.when: Compare mutually exclusive projects with unequal lives that will be replaced (EAB if benefits, EAC if costs).
formulas.trap: Use each project's own N in the annuity factor; for costs the smaller annual cost wins.

formulas.name: Constant chain of replacement (NPV to infinity)
formulas.when: Same comparison as EAV, replacing each project forever; consistent with the LCM method.
formulas.trap: In the LCM method repeat the whole NPV at each replacement; CCR and EAV always rank the projects the same way.

questions.stem: You are considering investing in a project which is expected to provide $215,000 net income per year for each of the next eight years, in return for an up-front investment of $1.2 million. You expect the residual value will be $0.96 million at the end. Your discount rate is 12% per annum. There is no tax. Determine each of the following and state the decision that arises from each figure: (a) accounting rate of return; (b) NPV. Enter part (a), the accounting rate of return, in % per annum.
solution: Average annual profit after tax = $215,000 (there is no tax, so net income is the profit after tax).
Average investment = (I0 + book value at the end)/2 = ($1,200,000 + $960,000)/2 = $1,080,000.

Decision: ARR gives only a relative signal. Accept if 19.91% beats the firm's target or the ROC of its other projects. It is a ratio of accounting figures, so it must not be compared with the 12% discount rate. The accept/reject call for this project comes from the NPV in part (b).

errors.label: Divided by the up-front investment
errors.explain: ARR divides by the AVERAGE investment (I0 + residual)/2, not by I0 alone.

errors.label: Divided by the residual value
errors.explain: The residual is only the closing book value; the average investment is the mean of the opening and closing book values.

errors.label: Forgot to halve the sum
errors.explain: (I0 + residual) is the sum of two book values; divide it by 2 to get the average.

questions.explanation: ARR = average annual profit after tax / average investment, with average investment = (I0 + residual book value)/2 = $1,080,000 here. The tempting I0 denominator ignores that the asset is written down over the project.

questions.stem: Prairie Ridge Dairy will install a $840,000 pasteurizing line, depreciated straight-line to zero over five years. Expected profits after tax are $94,000, $131,000, $157,000, $142,000 and $104,000 in years 1 to 5. What is the project's accounting rate of return (ROC) in % per annum?
solution: The line is written down to zero, so average investment = (840,000 + 0)/2 = $420,000.

errors.label: Divided by the full $840,000
errors.explain: With straight-line depreciation to zero the average book value is half the cost, $420,000.

errors.label: Used total profit instead of average profit
errors.explain: ARR uses the AVERAGE annual profit; the five-year total overstates the rate fivefold.

questions.explanation: ARR averages the profit over the life and divides by the average book value. Straight-line depreciation to zero makes the average investment half of the cost.

questions.stem: Similkameen Winery buys a $600,000 bottling line with a residual book value of $120,000 after six years (straight-line depreciation). It adds $150,000 a year to earnings before depreciation and tax. The tax rate is 30%. Find the ARR (ROC) in % per annum.
solution: Profit after tax = (150,000 - 80,000)(1 - 0.30) = $49,000. (ARR uses profit, not cash flow.)

errors.label: Used after-tax cash flow instead of profit
errors.explain: Cash flow (profit + depreciation = $129,000) is not accounting profit; ARR uses profit after tax.

errors.label: Divided by the original $600,000
errors.explain: The denominator is the average investment, $360,000.

errors.label: Used profit before tax
errors.explain: The rule uses profit AFTER tax: $70,000 x (1 - 0.30) = $49,000.

questions.explanation: Build profit after tax first (EBIT x (1 - T)), then divide by the average of the opening and residual book values.

questions.stem: Okanagan Orchards expects a new packing line to add $64,000 of profit after tax each year for five years. The line costs $500,000 and will have a book value of $100,000 at the end of year 5. What is its ARR (ROC)?
questions.explanation: Average investment = (500,000 + 100,000)/2 = $300,000, so ARR = 64,000/300,000 = 21.33%. 12.80% divides by I0 alone; 32.00% uses (I0 - residual)/2 = $200,000, which is half the depreciable amount, not the average book value; 16.00% divides by the depreciable amount $400,000.

questions.stem: A $800,000 sorting system at Fraser Valley Packaging is depreciated straight-line to zero over four years. Each year revenue is $520,000, cash costs are $300,000 and the tax rate is 25%. What is the ARR (ROC)?
questions.explanation: Profit after tax = (520,000 - 300,000 - 200,000)(0.75) = $15,000. Average investment = $400,000. ARR = 15,000/400,000 = 3.75%. 53.75% divides cash flow ($215,000) instead of profit; 26.88% divides cash flow by I0; 1.88% divides profit by I0.

questions.stem: The accounting rate of return on capital (ROC) of a project is:
options: expected average annual cash flow divided by the initial investment
the discount rate at which the NPV of the project is zero
the final-year profit divided by the cost of the asset
expected average annual profit after tax divided by average investment
questions.explanation: ROC = average annual profit after tax / average investment (capitalization). It uses accounting profit and book values, not cash flows, and is not a discount rate.

questions.stem: The board of Banff Springs Spa compares a proposed sauna wing with its other spa projects by dividing the wing's expected average annual profit after tax by the average of its cost and its book value at the end of the project. Which decision rule is the board using?
options: Internal rate of return
Profitability index
Accounting rate of return (ROC)
Payback period
questions.explanation: Average profit after tax over the average of the opening and closing book values is the ROC form of the ARR. No cash flows are discounted, so it is not IRR or PI, and nothing is measured in years, so it is not payback.

questions.stem: How does the ARR differ from the IRR?
options: ARR discounts the cash flows at the required return; IRR leaves them undiscounted and uses book values
ARR divides average accounting profit by average book value; IRR is the discount rate that makes the NPV zero
ARR is built from cash flows and the time value of money; IRR is built from accounting profit
ARR gives an absolute accept/reject decision against R; IRR gives only a relative comparison with other projects
questions.explanation: ARR = accounting profit / book value with no time value of money. IRR is built from cash flows and the time value of money and is compared with the required return R. The reverse statements swap the two rules.

questions.stem: All of the following are bad points of the accounting rate of return EXCEPT:
options: it uses accounting figures rather than cash flows
it ignores the time value of money
it is quick and easy to calculate
it uses single-year averages of a multi-year project
questions.explanation: Quick and easy calculation is the one good point of ARR. The bad points are accounting-based inputs (possibly including accruals), no time value of money, averaging, and no mechanism for an absolute decision.

questions.stem: Why does the ARR provide no mechanism for an absolute accept/reject decision on a single project?
options: it is expressed in dollars rather than as a rate, so it cannot be compared with R
it always equals the IRR for conventional cash flows, so it adds nothing to the IRR rule
it can only be calculated for projects with several IRRs, which makes any decision ambiguous
it is an accounting ratio with no market benchmark, so it can only be judged against other projects or a target
questions.explanation: ARR is not a rate of return in the economic sense: book profit over book value ignores timing. Without a market benchmark such as R, the rule can only rank a project against the ROC of the firm's other projects (a relative comparison).

questions.stem: A project's ROC is 19.9% and the firm's required return is 12%. An analyst says: "19.9% beats 12%, so accept." What is the best response?
options: ARR is an accounting ratio, so it cannot be tested against R; use NPV to decide whether to accept
Correct: any rate of return above the required return means a positive NPV
Correct, because ARR is calculated from the same discounted cash flows as the IRR
Incorrect: the project must be rejected because ARR ignores the residual value of the asset
questions.explanation: ARR is built from book profit and book values, with no discounting, so a number above R proves nothing about NPV. Compare ARR with other projects' ROC and make the accept decision with NPV.

questions.stem: In the ROC version of the ARR, "average investment" is:
options: the initial investment alone
the initial investment minus the residual value
the total of all annual profits divided by the number of years
(initial investment + book value at the end of the project)/2
questions.explanation: Average investment = (I0 + closing book value)/2: the mean of the opening and closing book values. With depreciation to zero it equals I0/2.

questions.stem: ROC, ROE and ROA are all accounting rates of return that differ only in the denominator: average capitalization, average book equity and average assets respectively.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: All three divide expected average annual profit after tax by an average book figure. ROC (average investment or capitalization) is the most common because it links to the capital put into the project.

questions.stem: The most common ARR is the _____ because it links with the idea of investing capital into the project.
options: ROE
ROA
ROC
EPS
questions.explanation: ROC (return on capital) divides average profit after tax by average investment or capitalization; it is the version that mirrors the capital committed to the project.

questions.stem: Westlock Foods will spend $135,000 on a new cold-storage unit. The unit is expected to produce cash flows of $25,000, $40,000, $45,000, $60,000 and $70,000 in years 1 to 5. What is the payback period in years?

steps.label: Still to recover at the end of year 3

solution: Cumulative flows: year 1 = 25,000; year 2 = 65,000; year 3 = 110,000; year 4 = 170,000.
The $135,000 is recovered during year 4. Still to recover after year 3 = 135,000 - 110,000 = $25,000.
Fraction of year 4 needed = 25,000/60,000 (year 4's cash flow) = 0.4167.

errors.label: Counted the whole recovery year
errors.explain: Payback is the year before recovery plus the fraction of the recovery year actually needed, not the end of the recovery year.

errors.label: Divided by the previous year's flow
errors.explain: The fraction is remaining ÷ the cash flow of the year in which recovery happens (year 4: $60,000).

errors.label: Cost divided by the average annual flow
errors.explain: Cost ÷ average flow is the annuity shortcut; it only works when the flows are equal.

questions.explanation: Payback = whole years before recovery + (unrecovered amount ÷ next year's cash flow).

questions.stem: Medicine Hat Machining is considering a $192,000 laser cutter that will return $71,500, $83,200 and $98,700 in years 1 to 3. The firm accepts projects that pay back within three years. Find the payback period in years (the project is then accepted or rejected against the cutoff).
solution: After year 2 the firm has recovered 71,500 + 83,200 = $154,700.
Still to recover = 192,000 - 154,700 = $37,300, which comes in year 3.
2.38 years < 3-year cutoff, so the rule says accept.

errors.label: Counted the whole recovery year
errors.explain: Year 3 is only partly needed; use the fraction 37,300/98,700.

errors.label: Divided by the previous year's flow
errors.explain: Use the cash flow of the recovery year (year 3), not year 2.

errors.label: Gave only the fraction of the year
errors.explain: Payback includes the whole years already elapsed: 2 + 0.378.

questions.explanation: Whole years until the cumulative flow is just short of the cost, plus remaining ÷ the next year's flow. Compare with the cutoff.

questions.stem: A $1,370,000 water-treatment upgrade at Red Deer Utilities is expected to save $285,000 in cash every year for 8 years. What is the payback period in years?
solution: The flows are an annuity, so payback = initial cost / annual cash flow.
Payback = 1,370,000 / 285,000 = 4.81 years (< 8-year life, so the project does pay back).

errors.label: Rounded up to the whole year
errors.explain: Payback includes the fraction of the recovery year: 4.81, not 5.

errors.label: Inverted the ratio
errors.explain: Payback is cost divided by the annual flow (years), not the flow divided by the cost (that is a yield).

questions.explanation: For level annual flows, payback = cost ÷ annual flow. Check that the result is less than the project's life.

questions.stem: Yellowhead Plastics pays $64,000 for a moulding press that returns $14,500, $18,200, $21,300, $24,900 and $26,000 in years 1 to 5. What is the payback period?
options: 4.00 years
3.40 years
3.47 years
0.40 years
questions.explanation: Cumulative flows: 14,500; 32,700; 54,000; 78,900. After year 3, 64,000 - 54,000 = 10,000 remains, recovered in year 4: 10,000/24,900 = 0.40, so payback = 3.40 years. 4.00 counts the entire recovery year; 3.47 divides by the previous year's flow ($21,300); 0.40 forgets the three whole years.

questions.stem: A $48,000 irrigation system at Taber Growers will return $6,000 at the end of each year for 7 years and then be worthless. What is its payback period?
options: The project never pays back
8.00 years
7.00 years
0.88 years
questions.explanation: Seven flows of $6,000 total $42,000, which is less than the $48,000 cost, so the investment is never recovered. 48,000/6,000 = 8.00 is the annuity shortcut applied beyond the 7-year life, where it does not make sense; 7.00 is simply the life; 0.88 divides the total inflows by the cost (an inverted ratio).

questions.stem: Wetaskiwin Dairy sets a 3-year payback cutoff. Project A costs $60,000 and returns $23,000, $28,000 and $21,000 in years 1 to 3. Project B costs $66,000 and returns $15,000, $18,000, $26,000 and $30,000 in years 1 to 4. Which statement is correct?
options: A pays back in 3.00 years and is accepted; B pays back in 4.00 years and is rejected
A pays back in 2.43 years and is accepted; B pays back in 3.23 years and is rejected
A pays back in 2.32 years and is accepted; B pays back in 3.27 years and is rejected
A pays back in 0.43 years and is accepted; B pays back in 0.23 years and is accepted
questions.explanation: A: after 2 years 51,000 is recovered, 9,000 remains, and year 3 brings 21,000: 2 + 9,000/21,000 = 2.43 < 3, accept. B: after 3 years 59,000 is recovered, 7,000 remains, and year 4 brings 30,000: 3 + 7,000/30,000 = 3.23 > 3, reject. The other options count whole recovery years, divide by the previous year's flow, or report only the fraction.

questions.stem: The payback period of a project is:
options: the length of time until the sum of its undiscounted cash flows equals the initial investment
the length of time until the sum of its discounted cash flows equals the initial investment
the number of years the project is expected to last
the discount rate that makes the NPV of the project zero
questions.explanation: Payback adds raw cash flows year by year until the initial outlay is recovered (part years allowed). Adding discounted flows would be the discounted payback.

questions.stem: Mackenzie Fitness Supply funds a new machine only if the cash it generates will repay the purchase price within three years, and it does not look at anything that happens after year 3. Which decision rule is it applying?
options: Discounted payback
Accounting rate of return
Payback period
Net present value
questions.explanation: Counting only whether undiscounted cash flows repay the cost within a year cutoff is the payback rule. Discounted payback would first convert each flow to its present value at R.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between the payback period and the discounted payback period?
options: Payback uses accounting profit; discounted payback uses cash flow
Payback gives an absolute accept/reject decision; discounted payback is only relative
Payback counts the cash flows after the payback date; discounted payback ignores them
Payback adds up raw cash flows; discounted payback adds up cash flows after discounting each at R
questions.explanation: Both rules are relative comparisons against a cutoff and both ignore flows after payback. Only the discounted version brings in the time value of money by using CF/(1+R)^t.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a bad point of the payback rule?
options: the mathematics is difficult
it ignores the time value of money
it ignores income after the payback period
it gives only a relative comparison, not an absolute decision
questions.explanation: Payback's good point is easy maths and speed. Its bad points are no time value of money, no credit for cash flows after the payback date, and no absolute decision (the cutoff is arbitrary).

questions.stem: Why does the payback rule bias a firm toward short-lived projects?
options: it discounts distant cash flows at a high rate, so later inflows count for little
it ignores cash flows after the payback date, so long projects get no credit for later inflows
it uses profit after tax, which is highest in the early years of a project
it assumes the cash flows are reinvested at the IRR rather than at R
questions.explanation: Payback only asks how fast the investment is recovered. Any large inflows that arrive after the cutoff are invisible, so a quickly recovered but short project can beat a longer, more valuable one.

questions.stem: At a 2-year payback cutoff, Cedar Valley Brewing accepts Short (cost $300,000; $120,000 then $200,000) and rejects Long (cost $300,000; $110,000 a year for 4 years). At R = 15%, NPV(Short) = -$44,423 and NPV(Long) = +$14,048. What does this show?
options: Payback and NPV always agree when the cutoff is set at two years or less
Short is better because its NPV is closer to zero than the NPV of Long
The cutoff was too long; a one-year cutoff would remove the conflict
Payback can accept a value-losing project and reject a value-adding one
questions.explanation: A payback below the cutoff is not a guarantee of positive NPV. Short pays back in 1.9 years but its flows are worth less than the cost at 15%. Long's payback of 2.73 years fails the cutoff even though its fourth year of income creates value. Changing the cutoff cannot fix a rule that ignores TVM.

questions.stem: When a project's cost is recovered partway through year k + 1, the fractional part of the payback period is:
options: the amount still unrecovered at the end of year k divided by the cash flow in year k
the cash flow in year k + 1 divided by the initial investment
the amount still unrecovered at the end of year k divided by the cash flow in year k + 1
the amount still unrecovered divided by the total of all remaining cash flows
questions.explanation: Payback = k + (remaining at end of year k)/CF(k+1). Dividing by year k's flow (the previous year) is a typical slip.

questions.stem: A project whose payback period is shorter than its life must have a positive NPV at any positive discount rate.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A payback shorter than the life only guarantees a positive NPV at a zero discount rate. At positive rates the NPV may be positive, zero or negative depending on whether R is below, equal to, or above the IRR.

questions.stem: If the cumulative cash flows of a project never reach its initial investment, the project has no payback period (it never pays back).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Payback is the time to recover the outlay. If the inflows over the whole life total less than the outlay, recovery never happens, and no fraction of a year can be computed.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes how to compute a payback period for uneven cash flows?
options: Discount each cash flow; cumulate the discounted flows; find the recovery year; divide by the number of years
Average the annual cash flows; divide the investment by this average; round up to the next whole year
Find the recovery year; add its cash flow to the investment; divide the total by the project life
Cumulate the cash flows; find the recovery year; divide the unrecovered amount by that year's flow; add the whole years before it
questions.explanation: Payback uses undiscounted flows: cumulate them, locate the year of recovery, take (remaining ÷ that year's flow) as the fraction, and add the completed years before it.

questions.stem: Two machines each cost $90,000. Machine X returns $50,000 in year 1 and $50,000 in year 2. Machine Y returns $20,000 a year for 15 years. The firm accepts anything with payback of 3 years or less. What does payback say?
options: Accept X (1.80 years), reject Y (4.50 years), although Y's total inflow is larger
Accept Y, because its cash flows last longer and total more than X's
Accept both, because both recover their cost eventually within their lives
Reject both, because neither pays back within a single year
questions.explanation: X: 50,000 after year 1, 40,000 remains, 40,000/50,000 = 0.8, so 1.80 years. Y: 90,000/20,000 = 4.50 years. Payback ignores Y's 15 years of inflows, which is the bias toward short projects.

questions.stem: Stony Plain Packaging pays $64,000 for a labelling line that will return $22,000, $26,500, $24,800, $23,000 and $21,500 in years 1 to 5. The required return is 13% per annum. What is the discounted payback period in years?

steps.label: Still to recover after year 3 (in PV terms)
PV of the year-4 cash flow

solution: Cumulative PV after year 3 = 57,410.06, so 64,000 - 57,410.06 = 6,589.94 is still to recover.

errors.label: Used undiscounted cash flows (ordinary payback)
errors.explain: That is the ordinary payback of 2.63 years. Discounted payback first converts each flow to its present value.

errors.label: Counted the whole recovery year
errors.explain: Add only the fraction of year 4 that is needed.

errors.label: Divided the discounted remainder by the undiscounted year-4 flow
errors.explain: Both parts must be in present-value terms: use the PV of the year-4 flow, $14,106.33.

questions.explanation: Discount every flow at R, accumulate the PVs, and find where they reach the cost; the fraction is (PV still to recover) ÷ (PV of the next year's flow).

questions.stem: Lacombe Brewing invests $41,000 in a bottling upgrade with cash flows of $12,800, $14,900, $17,400 and $19,100 in years 1 to 4. Its required return is 11% per annum and it accepts projects with a discounted payback of 3.5 years or less. Find the discounted payback in years.
solution: 3.37 < 3.5 years, so the rule says accept (the ordinary payback is 2.76 years).

errors.label: Used undiscounted flows
errors.explain: That gives the ordinary payback, 2.76 years, which ignores the time value of money.

errors.label: Divided the PV remainder by the undiscounted year-4 flow
errors.explain: The denominator must be the PV of the year-4 flow, $12,581.76, not $19,100.

questions.explanation: Discounted payback is always at least the ordinary payback for conventional flows and R > 0. Here it is 3.37 vs 2.76 years.

questions.stem: A $9,600 phone-system project at Spruce Grove Insurance returns $3,400, $3,900, $4,300 and $4,000 in years 1 to 4. The required return is 12% per annum. By how many years does the discounted payback exceed the ordinary payback?
solution: Ordinary payback: after two years 3,400 + 3,900 = 7,300; 2,300 remains; 2,300/4,300 = 0.535, so 2.53 years.
Cumulative PV after year 3 = 9,205.43, which is still short of 9,600 by 394.57. Recovery occurs in year 4: 394.57/2,542.07 = 0.155.

errors.label: Took the discounted recovery year as a whole year (4.00)
errors.explain: Discounted payback of 3.16 years includes only the fraction of year 4 that is needed.

errors.label: Gave the discounted payback itself, not the difference
errors.explain: The question asks for the excess of the discounted payback over the ordinary payback.

questions.explanation: Discounting shrinks later flows, so the cost is recovered later: discounted payback > ordinary payback for conventional flows and R > 0.

questions.stem: A $30,000 CNC upgrade returns $11,000, $12,500, $14,000 and $9,000 in years 1 to 4. The required return is 8% per annum. What is the discounted payback period?
options: 2.46 years
2.82 years
3.00 years
2.65 years
questions.explanation: PVs: 10,185.19; 10,716.74; 11,113.65. After 2 years 20,901.93 is recovered and 9,098.07 remains: 2 + 9,098.07/11,113.65 = 2.82 years. 2.46 uses undiscounted flows (ordinary payback); 3.00 counts the whole recovery year; 2.65 divides the PV remainder by the undiscounted year-3 flow ($14,000).

questions.stem: A project costs $9,000 and returns $2,000 at the end of each of the next 6 years. The required return is 18% per annum. What is the discounted payback period?
options: 4.50 years
6.00 years
It never pays back within the 6 years
10.03 years
questions.explanation: The PV of six $2,000 flows at 18% is 2,000 x 3.4976 = $6,995, which is less than $9,000, so the cost is never recovered in PV terms. 4.50 years is the ordinary payback; 6.00 is just the life; 10.03 solves the annuity equation as if the flows continued beyond year 6.

questions.stem: The discounted payback period is the length of time until:
options: the sum of the undiscounted cash flows equals the initial investment
the NPV of the project first becomes zero at the IRR
the sum of the present values of the cash flows equals the initial investment
accounting profit equals the book value of the asset
questions.explanation: Discounted payback uses CF/(1+R)^t for each year, so it measures the time to recover the investment in economic (present-value) terms.

questions.stem: Athabasca Tech asks how long it takes for the PV of a server upgrade's cash flows, discounted at the firm's 10% required return, to repay the purchase price, and accepts projects that do this within four years. Which rule is this?
options: Discounted payback
Payback period
Profitability index
Accounting rate of return
questions.explanation: Discounting each flow at R and then looking for the recovery year is the discounted payback. Without discounting it would be the ordinary payback.

questions.stem: For a conventional project and a positive discount rate, how does the discounted payback compare with the ordinary payback?
options: It is shorter, because discounting adds interest to each cash flow
It is longer, because discounting makes each future cash flow worth less
It is the same, because both use the same cash flows
It can be longer or shorter depending on the project life
questions.explanation: Each discounted flow is smaller than the raw flow, so more time is needed to recover the same cost. At R = 0 the two are equal. Discounted payback is therefore never shorter for conventional flows.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true of the discounted payback rule?
options: it takes into account the time value of money
it gives only a relative comparison, not an absolute decision
it ignores income beyond the discounted payback period
it takes into account the cash flows that occur after the discounted payback period
questions.explanation: Discounted payback fixes the time-value criticism but still ignores every cash flow after the recovery date and still needs a cutoff. Only the claim that it counts the cash flows after the discounted payback date is false.

questions.stem: Why is the following statement true: "If a project's discounted payback is shorter than its life, its NPV must be positive"?
options: discounted payback is calculated at the IRR rather than at the required return R
the ordinary payback is always shorter than the discounted payback, so NPV is positive
once the PV of the inflows has covered the cost inside the life, later discounted inflows only add to it
the discounted payback rule ignores the cost of the project and counts only the inflows
questions.explanation: Discounted payback uses the same R as the NPV. If the discounted flows have repaid the cost within the life, the sum of all discounted flows exceeds the cost, which is NPV > 0. (Ordinary payback gives no such guarantee.)

questions.stem: A project with conventional cash flows has a 5-year life, a discounted payback of 4.2 years at the firm's 14% required return and an ordinary payback of 3.1 years. What can be concluded?
options: The NPV is negative because the discounted payback is longer than the ordinary payback
The NPV is positive at 14% and the IRR exceeds 14%
Nothing, because payback rules give no information about NPV
The IRR is less than 14% because the discounted payback exceeds 4 years
questions.explanation: A discounted payback shorter than the life (4.2 < 5) means the PV of the inflows exceeds the cost, so NPV > 0 at 14%, and a positive NPV means the IRR is higher than 14%. The longer discounted payback is expected for any positive R.

questions.stem: To find a discounted payback you accumulate which quantity year by year until it equals the initial investment?
options: CF_t
CF_t × (1 + R)^t
CF_t/(1 + IRR)^t
CF_t/(1 + R)^t
questions.explanation: Each flow is brought back to time 0 at the required return R: CF_t/(1+R)^t. Using raw CF_t is the ordinary payback; compounding forward or using the IRR would not give a present value at R.

questions.stem: If the discount rate is 0%, a project's discounted payback period equals its ordinary payback period.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: At R = 0 each discount factor is 1, so the PV of every flow equals the flow itself and the two payback periods coincide.

questions.stem: The discounted payback rule gives an absolute accept/reject decision without a cutoff period.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It still compares the discounted payback with a pre-set limit, so it is only a relative comparison (and ignores cash flows after the recovery date).

questions.stem: You are considering investing in a project which is expected to provide $215,000 net income per year for each of the next eight years, in return for an up-front investment of $1.2 million. You expect the residual value will be $0.96 million at the end. Your discount rate is 12% per annum. There is no tax. Determine each of the following and state the decision that arises from each figure: (a) accounting rate of return; (b) NPV. For part (b) treat the $215,000 per year as the annual after-tax cash flow and the $0.96 million residual as cash received at the end of year 8. Enter part (b), the NPV, in $.
solution: PV of the eight annual flows = 215,000 x 4.967640 = $1,068,042.55.
Decision: NPV > 0, so accept. The project is expected to add about $255,770 to shareholder wealth.

errors.label: Ignored the residual value
errors.explain: The $960,000 residual is a cash inflow at the end of year 8 and must be discounted and added.

errors.label: Added the residual without discounting
errors.explain: The residual arrives in year 8, so it is worth 960,000/1.12^8 today.

errors.label: Discounted the up-front investment one year
errors.explain: The investment occurs today (t = 0) and is not discounted.

errors.label: Used a 7-year annuity factor
errors.explain: Eight annual flows need the 8-year annuity factor.

errors.label: Added back $30,000 straight-line depreciation to the flows
errors.explain: The question states the $215,000 is the annual cash flow, so no depreciation is added.

questions.explanation: NPV = CF0 + PV of the inflows (annuity plus the discounted residual). NPV > 0, so the project is accepted.

questions.stem: Beaumont Freight can buy a refrigerated trailer for $148,000. It is expected to generate cash flows of $52,400, $61,900 and $78,300 in years 1 to 3. The required return is 11% per annum. What is the NPV, and should the firm accept?

errors.label: Entered the outlay as a positive number
errors.explain: CF0 is an outflow, so it carries a minus sign: NPV = CF0 + PV with CF0 negative.

errors.label: Treated the outlay as year 1 (spreadsheet NPV() on the whole list)
errors.explain: The initial outlay is at t = 0; every later flow is at its own year number. Shifting everything one period divides the NPV by 1.11.

errors.label: Reported only the PV of the inflows
errors.explain: The PV of the inflows is not the NPV until you add the (negative) initial outlay.

questions.explanation: NPV = CF0 + sum of CF_t/(1+R)^t. A positive NPV means the project adds value at the 11% required return.

questions.stem: Cochrane Ridge Outfitters is evaluating a $420,000 store renovation with cash flows of $120,000, $135,000, $150,000 and $165,000 in years 1 to 4. Find the NPV at a required return of 9% per annum and at 16% per annum. Enter the NPV at 16%.
solution: Same cash flows, different required returns: the decision flips because NPV falls as R rises.

errors.label: Used +420,000 for the outlay
errors.explain: The outlay is a negative cash flow at t = 0.

errors.label: Used the 9% answer
errors.explain: The question asks for the NPV at 16%; at 9% the NPV is positive.

errors.label: Treated the outlay as year 1
errors.explain: Put the outlay at t = 0, with the first inflow at t = 1.

questions.explanation: Higher required returns shrink the PV of inflows, so NPV falls and a project can change from accept to reject without any change in its cash flows.

questions.stem: Camrose Wind Co. can build a turbine for $2,400,000. It is expected to generate $150,000 of cash flow next year, growing at 3% per annum forever. The required return is 9.5% per annum. What is the project's NPV?

steps.label: PV of the growing perpetuity D1/(R - g)

solution: Inflows are a growing perpetuity: PV = CF1/(R - g) = 150,000/(0.095 - 0.03) = $2,307,692.31.

errors.label: Added g to R in the denominator
errors.explain: The growing-perpetuity denominator is R - g.

errors.label: Reported the PV of the inflows only
errors.explain: Subtract the $2,400,000 outlay: NPV = CF0 + PV.

errors.label: Grew the first flow once more
errors.explain: The $150,000 is next year's flow (CF1), so it is not grown again.

questions.explanation: NPV = CF0 + CF1/(R - g) for a growing perpetuity; the same R - g logic as Gordon growth.

questions.stem: Bow Valley Logistics is considering a project with cash flows of -$260,000 now, then $90,000, $110,000 and $120,000 at the end of years 1 to 3. The required return is 12% per annum. What is the NPV?
questions.explanation: NPV = -260,000 + 90,000/1.12 + 110,000/1.12^2 + 120,000/1.12^3 = -$6,537.90, so reject. $513,462.10 adds the outlay as a positive number; $253,462.10 is just the PV of the inflows (CF0 left out); -$5,837.41 is the spreadsheet NPV() applied to the whole list (every flow shifted one period).

questions.stem: A $52,000 machine at Lloydminster Oilfield Services returns $14,000 at the end of each of the next 5 years. The required return is 10% per annum. What is the NPV?
options: None of the above
questions.explanation: PV of the annuity = 14,000 × 3.790787 = $53,071.01, so NPV = 53,071.01 − 52,000 = $1,071.01, which is not listed: none of the above. $53,071.01 forgets to subtract the outlay; $105,071.01 adds the outlay; $8,973.65 uses a 6-year annuity factor; $973.65 treats the outlay as a year-1 flow (the whole NPV divided by 1.10).

questions.stem: The net present value of a project is:
options: the discount rate at which the present value of the future cash flows equals the initial investment
the average annual accounting profit divided by the average investment
the present value of its future cash flows minus the initial investment (NPV = CF0 + PV, with CF0 negative)
the present value of the cash inflows divided by the present value of the cash outflows
questions.explanation: NPV = CF0 + PV with CF0 negative, so NPV = PV - initial investment. The rate that makes PV equal the cost is the IRR, average profit over average investment is the ARR, and PV of inflows over PV of outflows is the PI.

questions.stem: Camrose Fuels' CFO tells the board: "After discounting every expected cash flow at our 10% required return and subtracting the cost, this plant is expected to add $85,000 to the wealth of our shareholders." Which figure is she quoting?
options: Net present value
Internal rate of return
Profitability index
Discounted payback period
questions.explanation: A dollar amount equal to the change in shareholder wealth after allowing for the time value of money is the NPV. IRR and PI are not dollar amounts, and discounted payback is measured in years.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts NPV with IRR?
options: NPV is a percentage that must be compared with the required return; IRR is a dollar change in wealth
NPV is a dollar change in wealth measured at the required return; IRR is a percentage that must be compared with the required return
NPV ignores the time value of money; IRR includes it
NPV and IRR are always interchangeable, even for mutually exclusive projects
questions.explanation: NPV answers "how many dollars of wealth does this add?" IRR answers "what rate does it earn?". Both use the time value of money, but they can disagree on rankings and with unconventional flows.

questions.stem: All of the following are good points of the NPV rule EXCEPT:
options: it is the change in shareholder wealth
it uses the time value of money
it tells you how much value is created per dollar of capital tied up
it gives an absolute decision on each project as well as a relative comparison
questions.explanation: NPV does NOT consider the amount of capital tied up in the project; that is its bad point (the PI deals with it). Its good points are the link to shareholder wealth, the time value of money and an absolute decision.

questions.stem: Why does the NPV rule ensure the firm is doing the right thing for its shareholders?
options: NPV is the change in shareholder wealth, so NPV > 0 projects maximize the owners' value
NPV always selects the project with the highest percentage return on capital
NPV ignores uncertain future cash flows, which makes it the safest rule to use
NPV is the only rule that can be applied without forecasting any cash flows
questions.explanation: The financial manager's aim is to maximize shareholder wealth. Because NPV is exactly the expected change in that wealth (after the time value of money), it is the rule aligned with the goal.

questions.stem: A project has an NPV of +$12,000 at the firm's required return of 10%. What does that mean?
options: The project earns an accounting profit of $12,000 in each year of its life
After earning the 10% required return, the project adds $12,000 to shareholder wealth in today's dollars
The project recovers its cost from $12,000 of discounted cash flow each year
The project's IRR is 12%, which is above the 10% required return
questions.explanation: Positive NPV = value created beyond the required return, expressed in present-value dollars. It is not an annual profit, and NPV alone does not give the IRR.

questions.stem: Which expression gives the NPV of a project with CF0 = -100, CF1 = 60 and CF2 = 70 at discount rate R?
questions.explanation: CF0 occurs today so it is not discounted; CF1 is discounted once and CF2 twice. Dividing the -100 by (1+R) as well shifts everything one period (the spreadsheet NPV() trap); leaving the -100 out omits CF0; writing +100 flips its sign.

questions.stem: If a project's NPV is exactly zero, accepting it earns the firm exactly its required return and leaves shareholder wealth unchanged.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: NPV = 0 means the PV of inflows equals the cost; the project earns just the required return, so it neither adds nor destroys value.

questions.stem: A project with a negative NPV should never be undertaken under any circumstances.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A negative NPV is bad and the project is normally rejected, but firms are sometimes forced to carry out costly projects (for example restoring the environment after mining) where the least-negative NPV choice is taken.

questions.stem: An analyst types =NPV(12%, B2:B5) in a spreadsheet, where B2 holds the initial outlay of -$165,000 and B3:B5 hold the three annual inflows. What does the cell return?
options: The correct NPV, because the function includes the outlay at time 0 in B2
The PV of the three inflows only, because B2 is ignored as a label
A PV that treats the outlay as arriving in one year, so it equals the true NPV divided by 1.12
The IRR of the project, because the first value in the range is negative
questions.explanation: Excel's NPV() is really a PV(): it discounts the first value in the range by one period. The correct NPV is B2 + NPV(12%, B3:B5), with the outlay entered separately at t = 0.

questions.stem: Which sequence matches the professor's four-step analysis using NPV?
options: Choose the discount rate; decide accept or reject; estimate the cash flows; equalize unequal lives
Estimate the after-tax cash flows; choose the discount rate and discount to today; equalize unequal lives; decide accept or reject
Estimate the cash flows; compute the IRR; rank by IRR; decide accept or reject
Equalize unequal lives; estimate the cash flows; decide accept or reject; choose the discount rate
questions.explanation: Step 1 is the expected after-tax cash flows CF0, CF1, ...; step 2 is the discount rate R (or K) and discounting; step 3 is to make unequal lives comparable (EAV, CCR); step 4 is the accept/reject decision.

questions.stem: In the four-step NPV analysis, step 3 ("if comparing projects with unequal lives") asks you to:
options: make the lives equivalent, for example with EAV or a constant chain of replacement (CCR)
discount every cash flow at the IRR rather than at the required return R
drop the cash flows that occur after the shorter project has ended
choose the project with the longer life, because it earns more
questions.explanation: NPVs of projects with different lives are not comparable as they stand, so step 3 puts them on a common basis (EAV, CCR/NPV to infinity or the lowest common multiple of the lives).

questions.stem: Two mutually exclusive machines at Drumheller Mining cost the same but one lasts 3 years and the other 5. The analyst first converts each NPV into an equivalent annual value before choosing. Which step of the NPV sequence is this?
options: Step 1: estimate the after-tax cash flows
Step 2: choose the discount rate
Step 4(a): accept if NPV is positive
Step 3: equalize unequal lives
questions.explanation: Converting NPVs to EAVs (or using a constant chain of replacement) is how step 3 puts projects with unequal lives on the same footing before the accept/reject decision in step 4.

questions.stem: How does the step-4 decision differ between independent and mutually exclusive projects?
options: Independent: accept only the highest-NPV project; mutually exclusive: accept every project with a positive NPV
Independent: accept the highest IRR; mutually exclusive: accept the shortest payback
Independent: accept every project with NPV > 0; mutually exclusive: accept only the highest NPV (least negative if one must be taken)
There is no difference: both accept the single project with the highest NPV
questions.explanation: Independent projects do not affect each other, so each is judged on NPV > 0 alone. Mutually exclusive projects compete: only one can be taken, so choose the largest positive NPV.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four steps in the professor's NPV sequence?
options: rank the projects by their accounting rate of return
work out the expected after-tax cash flows
decide the discount rate and discount the cash flows to today
decide whether to accept or reject each project
questions.explanation: The NPV sequence uses cash flows, a discount rate, equalized lives where needed, and the NPV-based decision. Ranking by ARR belongs to a different (accounting) rule.

questions.stem: Why is step 1, estimating the after-tax cash flows, described as "not necessarily easy"?
options: the cash flows must first be converted into accounting profit before discounting
NPV is only as good as its forecasts: flows must be incremental, after tax and dated correctly
the cash flows should be measured before tax so that taxes do not distort them
the cash flows must be averaged over the life of the project before use
questions.explanation: Forecasting incremental after-tax cash flows (and choosing R) is the hard part of NPV; the arithmetic afterwards is mechanical. Accounting profit and averaging belong to the ARR, not NPV.

questions.stem: A mine must choose one of three mutually exclusive plans for restoring land that it is legally required to remediate. Their NPVs are -$840,000, -$615,000 and -$1,120,000. What does the NPV sequence say?
options: Reject all three, because every one of the NPVs is negative
Take the plan with NPV = -$1,120,000, because it spends the most money
Take all three plans, because they are independent of each other
Take the plan with NPV = -$615,000, the least negative, as one plan must be done
questions.explanation: Step 4(b): accept the highest NPV, or the least negative if you must take one. Forced projects (such as environmental repairs) are the case where a negative NPV is accepted.

questions.stem: Capilano Marine has three independent projects with NPVs of +$120,000, +$45,000 and -$30,000, and enough funds for all of them. Which should it accept?
options: Only the +$120,000 project, because it has the highest NPV
All three, because the total NPV is positive
The +$120,000 and +$45,000 projects only
None, because they cannot all have positive NPVs
questions.explanation: For independent projects the rule is NPV > 0 for each one separately. Accept +$120,000 and +$45,000 and reject -$30,000. (With limited funds this changes: capital rationing.)

questions.stem: For two mutually exclusive projects, NPV(P) = $15,154 and NPV(Q) = $14,523 at R = 10%, while IRR(P) = 18.9% and IRR(Q) = 23.2%. What does step 4(b) tell the firm to do?
options: Accept Q, because it has the higher IRR and so the higher return
Accept P, because mutually exclusive projects are ranked by NPV
Accept both, because both have positive NPVs at 10%
Accept neither, because the two IRRs differ from each other
questions.explanation: Step 4(b) uses NPV for mutually exclusive projects. The higher IRR of Q reflects its smaller scale; P adds $631 more to shareholder wealth.

questions.stem: Mutually exclusive projects at Sherwood Park Autobody: P costs $90,000 and returns $36,000, $44,000 and $48,000 in years 1 to 3; Q costs $60,000 and returns $29,000, $31,000 and $30,000. Both have 3-year lives and R = 10% per annum. Enter the NPV of the project that should be accepted.
solution: Same lives, so no equalizing is needed (step 3 skipped). Step 4(b): both positive but only one can be taken, so accept the higher NPV: P, at $15,154.02.

errors.label: Reported the NPV of Q (higher IRR)
errors.explain: Q has the higher IRR but a smaller NPV; for mutually exclusive projects choose the higher NPV.

errors.label: Entered P's outlay as a positive number
errors.explain: CF0 is an outflow: NPV = CF0 + PV with CF0 negative.

questions.explanation: NPV(P) > NPV(Q) > 0 at R = 10%. When projects are mutually exclusive, the highest positive NPV wins.

questions.stem: For independent projects, the NPV rule says to accept every project whose NPV is greater than zero.
options: True
False
