questions.explanation: Independent projects do not affect each other's values, so each is accepted if NPV > 0 (subject only to any resource constraint, which brings in capital rationing).

questions.stem: For mutually exclusive projects with equal lives, the NPV rule says to accept the project with the _____.
options: highest IRR
shortest payback
highest ARR
highest positive NPV
questions.explanation: Step 4(b): choose the highest positive NPV (the least negative if all are negative and one must be taken). Highest IRR, shortest payback and highest ARR are other rules that can give conflicting answers.

questions.stem: Using step 2 of the NPV sequence, a project costs $17,000 today and returns $9,000 at the end of year 1 and $12,000 at the end of year 2. The required return is 10% per annum. What is its NPV?
questions.explanation: NPV = -17,000 + 9,000/1.10 + 12,000/1.10^2 = -17,000 + 8,181.82 + 9,917.36 = +$1,099.17. $35,099.17 adds the outlay instead of subtracting it; $18,099.17 is the PV of the inflows only; $999.25 shifts every flow one period (outlay treated as year 1).

questions.stem: Wildrose Farms pays $250,000 today for a grain-drying operation that will be sold for a single payment of $338,000 in exactly 4 years. What is the project's IRR in % per annum?
solution: With one inflow, NPV = 0 means 250,000 = 338,000/(1 + IRR)^4.

errors.label: Forgot to subtract 1 after the root
errors.explain: The root gives 1 + IRR (the growth factor); subtract 1 to get the rate.

errors.label: Used the total gain without the root
errors.explain: 35.2% is the four-year total return; the IRR is the compound annual rate, found with the 4th root.

errors.label: Divided the total gain by 4
errors.explain: Dividing by N ignores compounding; use the Nth root.

questions.explanation: With one inflow, IRR = (inflow/outlay)^(1/N) - 1.

questions.stem: Cold Lake Aviation will pay $55,000 for avionics that return $33,000 at the end of year 1 and $36,500 at the end of year 2. The required return is 11% per annum. Find the IRR in % per annum (solve the quadratic) and decide.
solution: Decision: 16.81% > 11% required return, so accept (NPV at 11% = +$4,353.95, consistent).

errors.label: Averaged the net gain over the two years
errors.explain: Dividing the total net gain by the number of years ignores timing; the IRR discounts each flow.

errors.label: Average annual flow divided by the outlay
errors.explain: That is a cash yield on the outlay, not the discount rate that sets NPV to zero.

questions.explanation: For a two-year project let x = 1/(1+IRR) and solve CF0 + CF1 x + CF2 x^2 = 0. The calculator IRR key does the same by iteration.

questions.stem: Hay River Hotels pays $1,800,000 for a building that will produce net cash flow of $175,500 at the end of every year forever. The required return is 9% per annum. What is the project's IRR in % per annum?
solution: For a level perpetuity PV = CF/R. NPV = 0 means the cost equals CF/IRR.

errors.label: Inverted the ratio (a payback figure)
errors.explain: 1,800,000/175,500 = 10.26 is the payback in years, not a rate.

errors.label: Added the 9% required return to the yield
errors.explain: The cash yield already is the IRR for a level perpetuity; do not add the required return.

questions.explanation: For a level perpetuity, IRR = annual cash flow / initial outlay. It must beat R for a conventional project.

questions.stem: Kitscoty Storage pays $3,200,000 for a grain terminal expected to produce $252,000 of cash flow next year, growing at 2.5% per annum forever. What is the IRR in % per annum?
solution: For a growing perpetuity PV = CF1/(R - g). NPV = 0 means cost = CF1/(IRR - g).
IRR = 10.38% per annum (10.375%). Same structure as R = D1/P0 + g for a stock.

errors.label: Left out the growth rate g
errors.explain: The IRR is the cash yield plus the growth rate: CF1/cost + g.

errors.label: Subtracted g instead of adding it
errors.explain: Solve cost = CF1/(IRR - g) for IRR: IRR = CF1/cost + g.

questions.explanation: Growing-perpetuity IRR = CF1/cost + g, just as a stock's required return is D1/P0 + g.

questions.stem: A project costs $38,200 now and returns $14,900, $18,300 and $20,700 at the end of years 1 to 3. The required return is 12% per annum. What is its IRR?
questions.explanation: The IRR is the rate that sets NPV to zero; the calculator CF worksheet gives 18.26% (NPV is about $0.15 at 18.26% and +$4,426.07 at 12%). 13.70% is the total net gain divided by the cost and by 3 years (no compounding); 47.03% is the average annual flow divided by the cost; 12.00% is the required return, not the project's return.

questions.stem: A $96,000 project returns $31,000, $36,000, $41,000 and $27,000 at the end of years 1 to 4. The required return is 12% per annum. What is its IRR?
questions.explanation: Setting NPV to zero with the calculator worksheet gives 15.30% (NPV is about -$8 at 15.30% and +$6,719.53 at 12%, so IRR > R and the project is accepted). 10.16% averages the total net gain over four years; 35.16% divides the average flow by the cost; 12.00% is R.

questions.stem: The internal rate of return (IRR) of a project is:
options: the required return the firm needs to earn on the project
the average annual accounting profit divided by the average investment
the discount rate that makes the NPV of the project equal to zero
the present value of the inflows divided by the present value of the outflows
questions.explanation: IRR is the project's own return: the rate at which the PV of the future flows equals the price, i.e. NPV = 0. It is the same idea as the yield to maturity on a bond.

questions.stem: Hay River Lumber tells its lender that a new kiln "returns 14.2% on the money invested, the rate at which the present value of its cash flows exactly equals its cost." Which measure is that?
options: Required return (R)
Accounting rate of return
Profitability index
IRR
questions.explanation: The discount rate that sets the present value of the future cash flows equal to the cost is the IRR, the project's analogue of a bond's yield to maturity.

questions.stem: How should you distinguish IRR from the required return R?
options: IRR is what the project returns; R is the return the firm needs (its cost of capital)
IRR is the return the firm needs; R is what the project returns
IRR is an accounting measure; R is a cash-flow measure
They are the same number for any project that has a positive NPV
questions.explanation: IRR comes from the project's cash flows alone; R comes from the capital market and the project's risk. The rule compares them: IRR > R is good for conventional flows.

questions.stem: All of the following are good points of the IRR rule EXCEPT:
options: it uses the time value of money
it gives a single unambiguous rate for any pattern of cash flows
it shows the size of the return
it links with the NPV concept when the cash flows are conventional
questions.explanation: The bad point of IRR is that it may have multiple answers (or none) when the cash flows are unconventional. Good points: time value of money, shows the size of the return, agrees with NPV for conventional flows.

questions.stem: Why does IRR > R imply NPV > 0 for conventional cash flows?
options: the IRR is always calculated using the required return R as its discount rate
IRR and NPV are both measured in the same units, so they must agree
NPV falls as R rises and is zero at the IRR, so at any R below the IRR the NPV is positive
a conventional project always has an IRR above 100%, so its NPV is always positive
questions.explanation: For conventional flows the NPV profile slopes downward and crosses zero once, at the IRR. Any required return to the left of that crossing gives a positive NPV.

questions.stem: A project with conventional cash flows has an IRR of 17.18%. Firm A's required return is 12% and firm B's is 20%. What do the decision rules say?
options: Both accept, because the IRR is the same for every firm
Firm A rejects and firm B accepts, because a higher required return is more demanding
Both reject, because 17.18% is not above 20% for firm A
Firm A accepts (NPV > 0); firm B rejects (NPV < 0)
questions.explanation: The IRR is fixed by the cash flows; only R differs. Firm A has R < IRR, so NPV > 0; firm B has R > IRR, so NPV < 0. Reversing the comparison (accepting when IRR < R) swaps the decisions.

questions.stem: Which equation defines the IRR?
options: IRR = (CF1 + CF2 + ... + CFN)/CF0
IRR = PV of inflows / PV of outflows - 1
questions.explanation: IRR is the rate that makes NPV zero, and it appears inside the discount factors. Using R in the factors gives the NPV formula, not the IRR.

questions.stem: The IRR of a project is the same idea as the yield to maturity (YTM) of a bond: the discount rate that makes the present value of the future cash flows equal to the observed price.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: For a bond, YTM solves price = PV of coupons and face value; for a project IRR solves cost = PV of its inflows (NPV = 0).

questions.stem: The rule "accept if IRR > R" is valid for any pattern of cash flows.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It is only valid for conventional cash flows (CF0 negative, all later flows positive or zero). Unconventional flows can have several IRRs, none, or financing-type flows that reverse the rule.

questions.stem: A project with level cash flows that last forever has a payback period of 5 years. What is its IRR?
questions.explanation: For a perpetuity cost = CF/IRR, so payback = cost/CF = 1/IRR and IRR = 1/payback = 1/5 = 20%. (For long-lived projects with roughly constant flows, the shorter the payback, the higher the IRR.)

questions.stem: Moraine Lake Lodge is evaluating a $61,500 renovation with cash flows of $22,400, $27,900 and $31,450 in years 1 to 3. Compute the NPV at discount rates of 0%, 10% and 20% to sketch the NPV profile. Enter the NPV at 20%.
solution: NPV falls as R rises and changes sign between 10% and 20%, so the IRR is between 10% and 20% (it is 14.77%).

errors.label: Entered the outlay as a positive number
errors.explain: CF0 is an outflow; with CF0 positive the NPV is nonsense.

errors.label: Treated the outlay as year 1 (everything shifted one period)
errors.explain: The outlay is at t = 0 and is not discounted; shifting every flow divides the NPV by 1.20.

errors.label: Used the 10% result
errors.explain: The question asks for the NPV at 20%; at 10% the NPV is still positive.

questions.explanation: NPV profile points: NPV(0%) = sum of the flows; NPV falls as R rises; the profile crosses zero at the IRR.

questions.stem: A project costs $80,000 and returns $45,000 at the end of year 1 and $52,000 at the end of year 2. At what discount rate (% per annum) does its NPV profile cross the horizontal axis?
solution: The profile crosses the horizontal axis where NPV = 0, which is the IRR.
Check: at 10% NPV = +$3,884.30 and at 20% it is negative, so the crossing lies between them.

errors.label: Averaged the net gain over two years
errors.explain: That ignores the timing of the flows; the crossing point is the rate that discounts the flows to exactly $80,000.

errors.label: Average annual flow over the outlay
errors.explain: That is a cash yield, not the rate at which NPV = 0.

questions.explanation: The x-intercept of the NPV profile is the IRR. For a two-year project it can be found from the quadratic in x = 1/(1+IRR).

questions.stem: Peace River Mills is analyzing a $212,000 kiln with cash flows of $64,000, $71,500, $83,000 and $59,300 in years 1 to 4. What is the vertical intercept of its NPV profile (the NPV at a 0% discount rate)?
solution: At a 0% discount rate (and only then) cash flows can be added across time.

errors.label: Gave the sum of the inflows only
errors.explain: The vertical intercept is NPV, so subtract the outlay.

errors.label: Added the outlay
errors.explain: The outlay is an outflow and is negative.

errors.label: Discounted at 10%
errors.explain: At R = 0% there is no discounting; the 10% value is a different point on the profile.

questions.explanation: The vertical intercept of an NPV profile is the sum of the undiscounted cash flows, outlay included.

questions.stem: Moraine Lake Lodge's renovation costs $61,500 and returns $22,400, $27,900 and $31,450 in years 1 to 3. What is its NPV at a 15% required return?
questions.explanation: NPV(15%) = -61,500 + 22,400/1.15 + 27,900/1.15^2 + 31,450/1.15^3 = -$246.45, slightly negative because the IRR is 14.77%, just below 15%. $246.45 flips the sign; $5,550.34 is the NPV at 10%; $20,250.00 is the NPV at 0%.

questions.stem: For the same renovation (outlay $61,500; inflows $22,400, $27,900, $31,450), where does the NPV profile cross the vertical axis?
questions.explanation: On the vertical axis R = 0%, so NPV is the sum of all flows: -61,500 + 81,750 = +$20,250. +$81,750 forgets to subtract the outlay; -$61,500 is where the profile heads as R approaches infinity; +$143,250 adds the outlay.

questions.stem: An NPV profile is:
options: a table of the project's cash flows by year
a graph of the project's cumulative undiscounted cash flows over time
a plot of the project's IRR against its payback period
a graph of a project's NPV plotted against the discount rate
questions.explanation: The NPV profile shows how NPV changes as the discount rate varies. Its vertical intercept is the sum of the flows; where it crosses the horizontal axis is the IRR.

questions.stem: A graph for a conventional project shows NPV falling steadily from +$20,250 at R = 0% to -$13,445 at R = 30%, and cutting the horizontal axis at R = 14.77%. What does the crossing point represent?
options: The payback period
The required return
The IRR
The profitability index
questions.explanation: NPV = 0 at the point where the profile cuts the axis, so the discount rate there is the IRR. The required return is where you read the NPV for your firm; it is not a feature of the curve.

questions.stem: How does the NPV profile of a financing-type project (cash inflow first, outflows later) differ from that of a conventional investing project?
options: It slopes downward more steeply
It slopes upward (NPV rises with R) rather than downward
It is flat, because NPV does not depend on R
It always crosses the horizontal axis twice
questions.explanation: With the inflow at t = 0 and outflows later, a higher discount rate shrinks the PV of the outflows, so NPV rises with R. Conventional investing projects have the inflows later, so NPV falls with R.

questions.stem: Which statement about the NPV profile of a conventional project is NOT correct?
options: As the discount rate becomes very large, NPV approaches zero
It slopes downward as the discount rate rises
Its vertical intercept is the sum of the undiscounted cash flows
It crosses the horizontal axis once, at the IRR
questions.explanation: As R becomes very large the future flows are worth almost nothing, so NPV approaches CF0, the (negative) initial outlay, not zero.

questions.stem: Why does the NPV of a conventional project fall as the discount rate rises?
options: the inflows come after the outlay, so a higher rate shrinks their PV while the outlay at t = 0 is unchanged
a higher rate raises the present value of the outlay at t = 0 by more than that of the inflows
a higher rate compounds the later inflows into larger amounts that must be repaid
a higher rate shortens the payback period, which lowers the project's value
questions.explanation: NPV = CF0 + sum of CF_t/(1+R)^t. CF0 is not discounted, but every later inflow is divided by a larger factor as R rises, so the NPV decreases.

questions.stem: A conventional project's NPV profile crosses the horizontal axis at 14.77%. Firm A's required return is 12% and firm B's is 18%. What follows?
options: Both read a positive NPV, because the profile starts above zero
A reads a negative NPV and B a positive NPV, because the profile slopes upward
A reads a positive NPV and accepts; B reads a negative NPV and rejects
Neither can decide until the payback period is known
questions.explanation: The profile is above the axis to the left of the IRR (R < 14.77% gives NPV > 0) and below it to the right (R > 14.77% gives NPV < 0).

questions.stem: A project's NPV is +$12,307 at R = 5% and -$5,258 at R = 20%, with conventional flows. What does this tell you about its IRR?
options: The IRR is exactly 12.5%, because it is the average of the two rates
The IRR is below 5%, because the NPV is positive at a 5% discount rate
The IRR is above 20%, because the NPV is large and positive at 5%
The IRR is between 5% and 20%, because the profile changes sign between them
questions.explanation: A continuous downward-sloping profile that is positive at 5% and negative at 20% must cross zero between them; the exact crossing (the IRR) needs the full calculation, not an average of the two rates.

questions.stem: At a discount rate of 0%, the NPV of a project equals:
options: the sum of its inflows only, with the initial outlay excluded
the sum of all its cash flows, including the negative initial outlay
its initial outlay CF0, because the inflows are worth nothing
its IRR, because the discount rate is zero at that point
questions.explanation: With R = 0 every discount factor is 1, so NPV = CF0 + CF1 + ... + CFN. The initial outlay alone is the limit as R grows without bound.

questions.stem: For conventional cash flows, the NPV profile crosses the horizontal axis exactly once, at the project's IRR.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A conventional project (CF0 negative, later flows non-negative) has one sign change, so at most one IRR. The profile is downward sloping and crosses zero at that rate.

questions.stem: The NPV profile of every project slopes downward.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Projects with financing-type flows (inflow first, outflows later) have upward-sloping profiles, and unconventional flows can make the profile rise and then fall.

questions.stem: A quarry expansion at Exshaw Aggregates costs $500,000 now, generates $1,235,000 at the end of year 1, and requires $756,000 of site reclamation at the end of year 2. The cash flows change sign twice, so two IRRs exist. Find the LOWER IRR in % per annum.
keystrokes: CF0 = -500000, C01 = 1235000, F01 = 1, C02 = -756000, F02 = 1, IRR, CPT -> 12.00 (the calculator returns only one root, here depending on its guess)

errors.label: Gave the higher IRR instead
errors.explain: Both 12.00% and 35.00% make NPV = 0; the question asks for the lower one.

errors.label: Ignored the reclamation cost in year 2
errors.explain: The year-2 outflow is part of the cash flows and creates the second sign change.

questions.explanation: Two sign changes can give two IRRs. Both 12% and 35% satisfy NPV = 0; the calculator CF worksheet reports only one of them.

questions.stem: Using the same quarry expansion (outlay $500,000; $1,235,000 in year 1; reclamation cost $756,000 in year 2), the required return is 25% per annum. Compute the NPV, the figure that settles the decision.

steps.label: PV of the year-2 reclamation cost

solution: 25% lies between the two IRRs (12% and 35%), where the NPV is positive. Accept. A calculator that reports only 12% would wrongly say reject.

errors.label: Entered the outlay as a positive number
errors.explain: CF0 is an outflow.

errors.label: Treated the outlay as year 1
errors.explain: The outlay is at t = 0; shifting all flows divides the NPV by 1.25.

errors.label: Did not discount the year-2 cost
errors.explain: The reclamation cost occurs in year 2 and must be divided by 1.25^2.

questions.explanation: With multiple IRRs the NPV at the required return decides. The profile is positive only between the two IRRs.

questions.stem: A film-studio expansion at Okotoks Pictures costs $500,000 now, brings in $800,000 in year 1, then requires $400,000 of clean-up in year 2. The required return is 10% per annum. Find the NPV. (Its NPV is negative at every discount rate, so no real IRR exists.)
solution: The profile never reaches zero (its maximum is -$100,000), so NPV < 0 at every R: reject.

errors.label: Entered the outlay as a positive number
errors.explain: CF0 is an outflow.

errors.label: Did not discount the year-2 clean-up
errors.explain: The clean-up cost occurs in year 2 and must be divided by 1.10^2.

errors.label: Left out the clean-up cost
errors.explain: The year-2 outflow is part of the project.

questions.explanation: No real IRR does not mean the project is acceptable: always fall back on the NPV at R.

questions.stem: A project's cash flows are -$60,000, +$90,000, +$56,000 and -$90,000 in years 0 to 3. Its two IRRs are about 8.32% and 40.35%. The required return is 15%. Which statement is correct?
options: Reject: the calculator's IRR of 8.32% is below the 15% required return
Accept: NPV(15%) = +$1,428.45, although the calculator's first IRR (8.32%) is below 15%
Reject: NPV(15%) = -$1,428.45, since the cash flows end with an outflow
No decision is possible: with two IRRs neither the IRR nor the NPV rule gives an answer
questions.explanation: NPV(15%) = -60,000 + 90,000/1.15 + 56,000/1.15^2 - 90,000/1.15^3 = +$1,428.45. 15% lies between the two IRRs, where the NPV is positive. Trusting the single IRR the calculator shows (IRR below R, so reject) gives the wrong decision; having two IRRs does not stop the NPV from deciding.

questions.stem: For cash flows of -$500,000, +$1,235,000 and -$756,000 (IRRs of 12% and 35%), at which required returns is the project accepted?
options: Between 12% and 35%
Above 12%
Below 35%
Below 12%
questions.explanation: NPV is positive only between the two IRRs (for example +$4,160.00 at 25%). Below 12% the NPV is negative (-$2,066.12 at 10%), and above 35% it is negative again (-$3,571.43 at 40%). The one-sided answers each apply the conventional rule to a single IRR.

questions.stem: For the same cash flows (-$500,000, +$1,235,000, -$756,000), what is the NPV at a required return of 8%, below both IRRs?
questions.explanation: NPV(8%) = -500,000 + 1,235,000/1.08 - 756,000/1.08^2 = -$4,629.63. It is negative: a required return below both IRRs does NOT mean accept when the flows are unconventional. $4,160.00 is the NPV at 25%; -$2,066.12 is the NPV at 10%.

questions.stem: The "multiple IRR" problem refers to:
options: the same project having a different IRR for each firm that evaluates it
a project having several payback periods, one for each positive cash flow
the IRR changing each year as new cash flows are received
more than one discount rate making the project's NPV equal to zero
questions.explanation: When the cash flows change sign more than once, the NPV equation can cross the horizontal axis several times, so several rates solve NPV = 0.

questions.stem: A mining project costs $9 million now, earns positive cash flows for three years, and then requires a $4 million environmental clean-up in year 4. Its NPV equation crosses zero at two different rates. Which problem does this illustrate?
options: The scale problem in ranking projects
The timing problem in ranking projects
The reinvestment-rate problem of the IRR
Multiple IRRs from unconventional flows
questions.explanation: Flows that change sign more than once (a large cost late in the life) can produce more than one IRR. Scale and timing problems concern ranking mutually exclusive projects.

questions.stem: An analyst enters -$500,000, +$1,235,000 and -$756,000 in a financial calculator and sees a single IRR of 12.00%. She then plots the NPV profile and sees it cross the axis twice. What did the calculator do?
options: It averaged the two IRRs
It reported only one of the two IRRs
It reported the IRR that is closest to the required return
It reported the correct IRR; the second crossing is a plotting error
questions.explanation: Calculators and spreadsheets iterate from a starting guess and stop at the first root they find. The other IRR (35%) is just as valid, which is why the NPV profile, or the NPV at R, must be checked.

questions.stem: How do conventional and unconventional cash flows differ in terms of IRRs?
options: Conventional flows (one sign change) have one IRR; unconventional flows (several sign changes) can have several or none
Conventional flows can have several IRRs, while unconventional flows always have exactly one IRR
Both always have exactly one IRR; the two kinds differ only in the size of the NPV
Unconventional flows never have an IRR, so only the NPV can be used for them
questions.explanation: Conventional: CF0 negative and all later flows positive or zero, so a single sign change and a single crossing. Unconventional: mixed signs, so up to as many IRRs as there are sign changes (possibly none).

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a typical reason for unconventional cash flows?
options: an occasional year with large maintenance costs
clean-up or decommissioning costs at the end of the project
a single initial outlay followed by level positive annual inflows
the incremental cash flows of one project minus another
questions.explanation: A single outlay followed by positive inflows is the conventional pattern. Unconventional flows come from large later costs (maintenance, reclamation) and from incremental (A minus B) streams.

questions.stem: Why can a project with cash flows that change sign twice have two IRRs?
options: the firm has two different required returns, one for each sign of cash flow
the NPV is calculated twice, once before tax and once after tax
the IRR depends on the order in which the flows are entered into the calculator
solving NPV = 0 means finding the roots of an equation, and a curve that crosses the axis twice has two roots
questions.explanation: The IRR is a root of the NPV equation. Mixed-sign flows can make the NPV profile cross the axis more than once, and each crossing is an IRR (up to the number of sign changes).

questions.stem: Why can the difference between two conventional cash-flow streams (project A minus project B) have more than one IRR?
options: year-by-year subtraction can create several sign changes, i.e. an unconventional stream
subtracting always adds an extra year of cash flows to the difference
the difference is always negative in the last year of the project
the IRR of a difference between two projects is not defined at all
questions.explanation: Each stream may have one sign change, but their difference can swing between positive and negative from year to year. That is why incremental IRRs (crossover rates) need care.

questions.stem: A project with cash flows of -$500,000, +$1,235,000 and -$756,000 has IRRs of 12% and 35%. The required return is 8%. A manager says: "Both IRRs are above our 8%, so we accept." What is the right response?
options: Accept: both IRRs exceed the required return, so the NPV must be positive
Reject: the project has two IRRs, so its value cannot be determined at all
Reject: NPV(8%) = -$4,629.63; with unconventional flows IRR > R no longer implies NPV > 0
Accept: the NPV is positive at every discount rate below the higher IRR of 35%
questions.explanation: The NPV is negative below 12%, positive between 12% and 35%, and negative above 35%. R = 8% is in the negative zone even though both IRRs exceed it.

questions.stem: A project's cash flows are -$10M, +$1M, +$1M, +$1M, -$3M, +$1M, +$1M. What is the maximum number of IRRs it could have?
questions.explanation: The sign pattern -, +, +, +, -, +, + changes sign three times (- to +, + to -, - to +), so there may be up to three IRRs. Counting negative flows (two) or total flows would give the wrong bound.

questions.stem: The maximum number of IRRs a project can have is equal to:
options: the number of years in the project
the number of negative cash flows
the number of positive cash flows
the number of times its cash flows change sign
questions.explanation: Descartes' rule of signs bounds the number of real positive roots by the number of sign changes. It is an upper limit: there may be fewer, or none.

questions.stem: A project whose cash flows change sign exactly twice must have exactly two IRRs.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Two sign changes allow up to two IRRs. There can be one, two, or none: for example -500,000, +800,000, -400,000 has no real IRR.

questions.stem: When the IRR rule and the NPV rule conflict because of unconventional cash flows, the NPV rule should be used.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: NPV is unambiguous for any pattern of cash flows because it is a single value at the required return; the IRR can be multiple or missing.

questions.stem: A firm lists four proposals with cash flows in $ thousands at years 0, 1, 2 and 3. Which proposal has financing-type cash flows?
questions.explanation: Financing-type flows start with money coming IN (a positive CF0) and are followed by money going OUT. The proposal +95, −40, −40, −40 looks like a loan or a customer prepayment. The −120, +50, +50, +50 pattern is conventional, and −80, +60, −25, +70 changes sign twice (an unconventional mid-life cost), but neither starts positive and then only pays out.

questions.stem: In the professor's terms, a project has financing-type cash flows when:
options: CF0 is negative and the later cash flows are positive
the cash flows change sign more than twice
the cash flows include interest paid on the firm's debt
CF0 is positive (money received up front) and the later cash flows are negative
questions.explanation: Financing-type flows reverse the usual pattern: you receive cash first and pay it back later, like borrowing. A conventional project is the other way round. Interest on the firm's own debt is a financing cost that is kept OUT of project cash flows, so it is not what makes flows 'financing-type'.

questions.stem: How does the IRR decision rule for a financing-type project differ from the rule for a conventional project?
options: Conventional: accept if IRR > R. Financing-type: the same rule, because IRR is always a return.
Conventional: accept if IRR < R. Financing-type: accept if IRR > R.
Conventional: accept if IRR > R. Financing-type: accept if IRR < R.
Both use IRR > R, but financing-type projects must also have a payback under two years.
questions.explanation: For a conventional project the IRR is the return you earn, so you want it above R. For a financing-type project the IRR is the rate you PAY for the money received up front, so you want it below R. Applying the conventional rule to financing-type flows is the classic wrong-direction error.

questions.stem: Why does the IRR rule reverse for financing-type cash flows?
options: Financing-type flows have two IRRs, and the lower one must always be used
The later cash flows are negative, so the IRR must itself be negative
Financing-type projects are riskier, so the firm should demand a higher IRR
The IRR is the cost of the money received, and NPV rises with R as the later outflows shrink
questions.explanation: With a positive CF0 and negative later flows, a higher discount rate makes the future outflows cheaper in present value, so NPV climbs with R (an upward-sloping NPV profile). NPV is positive when R is above the IRR, which is the same as IRR below R. The sign pattern has one change, so there is a single IRR, and it is usually positive.

questions.stem: Northwind Cold Storage is paid $72,000 up front for a service contract and must spend $38,000 at the end of year 1 and $41,000 at the end of year 2. Its IRR is 6.33% per annum and the required return is 11%. What follows?
options: Reject: the IRR of 6.33% is below the required return of 11%
Reject: the later flows are negative, so the contract cannot create value
Accept only if the IRR is above 11%, so the answer cannot be decided
Accept: the contract funds the firm at 6.33%, below the 11% it requires, and NPV is positive
questions.explanation: The flows are financing-type, so the rule flips: accept when IRR < R. 6.33% < 11%, and the NPV at 11% is $4,489.25, which confirms it. Rejecting because 'IRR is below R' applies the conventional rule to flows it does not fit.

questions.stem: A project pays the firm $50,000 today and then costs $30,000 at the end of each of the next two years. The required return is 10% and the project's IRR is above 10%. The firm should accept it because the IRR exceeds the required return.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: These are financing-type flows, so an IRR above R means the money costs MORE than the firm can earn elsewhere. Check with NPV: 50,000 − 30,000 × annuity factor(10%, 2) = 50,000 − 30,000 × 1.73554 = −$2,066.12, so reject.

questions.stem: All of the following are true of a project with financing-type cash flows EXCEPT:
options: NPV falls as the required return rises
The IRR is a cost of funds rather than a return earned
The NPV profile slopes upward
The project should be accepted when IRR < R
questions.explanation: For financing-type flows the NPV profile slopes UP, so NPV rises (not falls) as R increases. The other three statements are the standard properties: IRR is the cost of the money received, the profile slopes upward, and the accept rule is IRR < R.

questions.stem: A project brings in $60,000 now and costs $35,000 at the end of each of the next two years. The NPV at 0% is −$10,000 and the IRR is 10.92%. For which required returns R should the firm accept it?
options: Any R below 10.92%
Any R above 0%, because the NPV at 0% is the only number that matters
Any R above 10.92%
Never: the NPV at 0% is negative
questions.explanation: Financing-type NPV starts negative at R = 0 and rises, crossing zero at the IRR of 10.92%. So NPV is positive, and the project acceptable, for every R above the IRR. Choosing 'below' reverses the rule.

questions.stem: Northwind Cold Storage is paid $72,000 up front and must spend $38,000 at the end of year 1 and $41,000 at the end of year 2. The required return is 11% per annum. What is the NPV? (Answer in $, to the cent.)
solution: CF0 = +72,000 (money received) and the later flows are negative.
NPV > 0, so accept (the IRR is below R, as the financing-type rule requires).

errors.label: Treated the up-front $72,000 as an outflow
errors.explain: The $72,000 is cash received, so CF0 is +72,000; flipping its sign makes everything negative.

errors.label: Discounted CF0 one period
errors.explain: CF0 occurs today and is not discounted; every later flow moves out one year in this error.

errors.label: Added the flows without discounting
errors.explain: At 0% the flows can be added, but the firm's required return is 11%, so each outflow must be discounted.

questions.explanation: Positive CF0 less the present value of the two later costs. The positive NPV says the up-front money is cheaper than the firm's 11% requirement.

questions.stem: A supplier offers to prepay $47,000 now in return for $52,000 of goods delivered in one year. The firm's required return is 12% per annum. First find the IRR of the deal, then its NPV. (Final answer: the NPV in $, to the cent.)
solution: IRR (10.64%) < R (12%) and NPV > 0, so accept: the funds cost less than the firm requires.

errors.label: Used −47,000 now and +52,000 later (conventional signs)
errors.explain: That is the NPV of lending the money, not of receiving it.

errors.label: Discounted both flows by a year
errors.explain: CF0 happens today (no discounting), and the repayment is one year away, not two.

errors.label: Subtracted the repayment without discounting
errors.explain: The $52,000 is paid in a year, so it must be discounted at 12% before comparing.

questions.explanation: A one-period financing deal has IRR = repayment/amount received − 1, here 10.64%. Because this cost is below 12%, NPV is positive and the deal is accepted.

questions.stem: A co-op receives $120,000 now and repays $52,000 at the end of each of the next three years. The required return is 10% per annum. What is the NPV? (Answer in $, to the cent.)
solution: Financing-type flows: +120,000 now, then −52,000 for three years.
NPV < 0 (the IRR of about 14.36% is above R = 10%), so reject: the money costs too much.

errors.label: Used a 4-year annuity factor
errors.explain: Three repayments need a three-year annuity factor.

errors.label: Put the $120,000 as an outflow
errors.explain: The $120,000 is received, so it enters as +120,000.

errors.label: Added the undiscounted repayments
errors.explain: Three payments of 52,000 are 156,000 undiscounted; at 10% their present value is smaller.

questions.explanation: The repayments are an ordinary annuity discounted at R and subtracted from the cash received. NPV is negative, so the firm rejects the financing. The IRR (14.36%) is above R, which for financing-type flows signals reject.

questions.stem: Maple Ridge Marinas receives a $30,000 grant now and must spend $16,000 at the end of year 1 and $17,500 at the end of year 2. At a required return of 9% per annum, what is the NPV?
questions.explanation: NPV = 30,000 − 16,000/1.09 − 17,500/1.09² = 30,000 − 14,678.90 − 14,729.40 = $591.70. The wrong figures come from treating the grant as a cost, discounting CF0 a year, or adding the flows undiscounted (−$3,500).

questions.stem: A firm receives $90,000 today and pays $50,000 at the end of each of the next two years. It correctly computes the IRR of the deal and compares it with its required return. For which required returns should it accept?
options: R above 7.32%
R below 7.32%
R above 11.11%
R below 11.11%
questions.explanation: Solve 90,000 = 50,000/(1 + r) + 50,000/(1 + r)²: the annuity factor must be 1.8, which gives r = 7.32%. The money costs 7.32% per annum, so accept only if the firm requires more than that. 11.11% is the undiscounted gain (100,000/90,000 − 1), which ignores the timing, and 'below' flips the rule.

questions.stem: A project has a positive CF0 followed by two negative cash flows. If the required return R rises from 6% to 12%, what happens to the NPV?
options: It falls, as for every conventional project
It stays the same, because the cash flows do not change
It rises, because the later outflows are discounted more heavily
It falls until the IRR and then rises
questions.explanation: NPV = CF0 + PV(later flows). With negative later flows, a higher R shrinks the present value of those costs, so NPV goes up. Northwind-type contracts show it: NPV is −$338.91 at 6% and +$5,386.48 at 12%.

questions.stem: A modified internal rate of return (MIRR) is:
options: the IRR after removing the project's largest cash flow
the IRR of cash flows that have first been modified using an external discount or reinvestment rate
the discount rate at which the project's discounted payback equals its life
the average of the project's IRRs when it has more than one
questions.explanation: An MIRR first rewrites the cash flows (discounting some to today, compounding others to the end, or both) and then takes the IRR of the modified flows. Because the modified flows have one sign change, there is a single answer.

questions.stem: To find an MIRR, an analyst discounts every negative flow back to time 0 at the required return, compounds every positive flow forward to the end of the project at the same rate, and then computes the IRR of the two resulting flows. Which approach is this?
options: The discounting approach
The reinvestment approach
The payback approach
The combination approach
questions.explanation: The combination approach does both things: negative flows are discounted to time 0 and positive flows are compounded to the end. The discounting approach only moves negative flows to time 0, and the reinvestment approach only compounds everything (except CF0) to the end.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly separates the ordinary IRR from an MIRR?
options: The MIRR depends only on the project's own cash flows, while the IRR needs a required return
Both are true internal rates because both set an NPV to zero
The IRR depends only on the project's own cash flows, while an MIRR also needs an externally supplied rate
The IRR assumes cash flows are reinvested at the required return; the MIRR does not reinvest anything
questions.explanation: The IRR is computed from the cash flows alone. An MIRR is not truly 'internal': it uses the required return (or a reinvestment rate) to rewrite the flows first, so the result changes if that rate changes. Neither IRR nor NPV actually requires a reinvestment assumption.

questions.stem: Why does an MIRR not suffer from the multiple-IRR problem?
options: The MIRR ignores all negative cash flows
The MIRR is always calculated at the required return, so it is never an IRR
The modified cash flows change sign only once, so only one IRR exists
The MIRR is computed on the project's NPV instead of its cash flows
questions.explanation: Discounting the later negative flows to time 0 (or compounding everything to the end) leaves a negative start and a positive finish, so the sign pattern is conventional and only one rate solves it. The cost is that the answer now depends on the rate used to modify the flows.

questions.stem: Cedar Creek Mining expects cash flows of −$80,000 now, +$45,000, +$52,000 and +$38,000 in years 1 to 3, and a −$30,000 reclamation cost in year 4. Use the combination approach at R = 10% per annum for both discounting and compounding. What is the MIRR? (% per annum, 2 decimals.)
solution: Discount the negative flows to time 0: 80,000 + 30,000/1.1⁴ = 100,490.40.

errors.label: Used the reinvestment approach instead
errors.explain: That approach leaves −$80,000 at time 0 and subtracts the −$30,000 from the year-4 value instead of discounting it, so it is a different MIRR.

errors.label: Added the reclamation cost to CF0 without discounting
errors.explain: The year-4 cost must be discounted four years at R before it joins the time-0 outflow.

errors.label: Took the cube root instead of the fourth root
errors.explain: The modified flows are four years apart (time 0 to time 4), so the root is 1/4.

questions.explanation: Combination approach: negatives to today, positives to the end, then a two-flow IRR. It is a two-flow problem, so a root, not a trial-and-error search, finishes it.

questions.stem: Ridgeline Quarry has cash flows of −$90,000 now, +$40,000 in year 1, −$15,000 in year 2, +$48,000 in year 3 and +$52,000 in year 4. Using the reinvestment approach with a reinvestment rate of 8% per annum, what is the MIRR? (% per annum, 2 decimals.)

steps.label: Time-4 value of every flow after time 0

solution: Reinvestment approach: compound every flow EXCEPT CF0 to the end (year 4) at 8%.

errors.label: Used the combination approach (negative flow discounted to time 0)
errors.explain: The reinvestment approach compounds the −$15,000 forward with everything else; it does not discount it to time 0.

errors.label: Used a three-year root
errors.explain: From time 0 to year 4 is four years, so the root is 1/4.

errors.label: Reported the growth factor 1.1102 as 111.02%
errors.explain: A rate is the growth factor minus 1.

questions.explanation: Reinvestment approach: carry every later flow, positive or negative, to the project's end at the reinvestment rate, then treat the result as a single investment and a single terminal value.

questions.stem: Cedar Creek Mining (−$80,000 now; +$45,000, +$52,000, +$38,000 in years 1 to 3; −$30,000 in year 4) uses R = 10% per annum. Using the DISCOUNTING approach (only the negative flows are moved, to time 0), what is the MIRR?
questions.explanation: Discounting approach: time-0 flow = −80,000 − 30,000/1.1⁴ = −100,490.40, with +45,000, +52,000 and +38,000 left in years 1 to 3. The IRR of those flows is 16.80%. 13.13% is the combination MIRR, 13.89% the reinvestment MIRR, and 21.17% the ordinary IRR of the original flows.

questions.stem: Cedar Creek Mining's combination-approach MIRR is 13.13% against a required return of 10%, and its NPV at 10% is $11,943.86. What should the analyst conclude?
options: Accept; MIRR and NPV agree, and if they ever disagreed the NPV rule would govern
Reject; the MIRR must be at least as high as the ordinary IRR of 21.17%
Accept only if the MIRR equals the required return exactly
No decision; an MIRR is the project's true internal return so it cannot be compared with R
questions.explanation: The MIRR (13.13%) exceeds R and the NPV is positive, so both say accept. The MIRR is not a true internal return, since it depends on the rate used to modify the flows, which is why NPV is the fall-back rule. The three methods give different MIRRs for the same project.

questions.stem: For a conventional project (a negative CF0 followed only by positive cash flows), the discounting-approach MIRR equals the ordinary IRR.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The discounting approach only moves NEGATIVE flows back to time 0. A conventional project has no negative flows after time 0, so its cash flows are left unchanged and the IRR of the 'modified' flows is the ordinary IRR. The reinvestment and combination approaches do change the flows, and give a different answer.

questions.stem: All of the following are common criticisms of the MIRR EXCEPT:
options: It is not a true internal rate, because it depends on externally supplied rates
There are several ways to calculate it and no clear reason to prefer one
If the relevant discount rate is known, the NPV can be calculated directly
It cannot be calculated when the cash flows change sign more than once
questions.explanation: The MIRR was invented to deal with cash flows that change sign more than once, because it always gives one answer. The criticisms are the other three: it is not internal, there are several competing versions, and NPV answers the same question without the extra steps.

questions.stem: A project costs $50,000 and returns $30,000 at the end of year 1 and $35,000 at the end of year 2. The reinvestment rate is 10% per annum. Which expression gives the reinvestment-approach MIRR?
questions.explanation: Compound each flow after time 0 to the end of the project (year 2): the year-1 flow grows one year at 10% and the year-2 flow is already at the end. Divide by the initial outlay and take the 2nd root. Compounding the wrong flow, compounding to year 3, or skipping the root all give wrong rates.

questions.stem: A project costs $50,000 and returns $30,000 at the end of year 1 and $35,000 at the end of year 2. Using the reinvestment approach at 10% per annum, what is the MIRR?
questions.explanation: Value at year 2 = 30,000 × 1.10 + 35,000 = 68,000; MIRR = (68,000/50,000)^(1/2) − 1 = 16.62%. 18.88% is the ordinary IRR, 36.00% forgets the square root, and 17.05% compounds the wrong flow.

questions.stem: Two mutually exclusive projects have IRRs of 24% and 21%. At the firm's required return of 10% the 21% project has the higher NPV. This disagreement between the IRR and NPV rankings is called:
options: the multiple-IRR problem
a ranking conflict between IRR and NPV
capital rationing
a financing-type cash-flow problem
questions.explanation: When IRR and NPV rank mutually exclusive projects differently, the firm faces a ranking conflict. It is caused by differences in scale or timing, not by unconventional cash flows (multiple IRRs), by a lack of funds (rationing), or by the sign pattern.

questions.stem: Why is NPV, not IRR, used to make the final choice between mutually exclusive projects?
options: IRR cannot be calculated when projects are mutually exclusive
NPV measures the change in shareholder wealth in dollars, so the highest NPV adds the most value
NPV is a percentage, so it can be compared across projects of different sizes
IRR is based on accounting profit while NPV is based on cash flows
questions.explanation: The financial manager's aim is to maximise shareholder wealth, and NPV is that change in wealth. IRR is a rate that ignores how many dollars are invested. Both IRR and NPV use cash flows, and NPV is a dollar amount, not a percentage.

questions.stem: Which pair identifies the two ways in which the IRR and NPV rankings of mutually exclusive projects can conflict?
options: The scale of the investment and the timing of the cash flows
The tax rate and the rate of inflation
The number of IRRs and the sign of CF0
The riskiness and the liquidity of the projects
questions.explanation: A bigger project can have a lower IRR yet a bigger NPV (scale), and a project with later cash flows can have a lower IRR yet a bigger NPV at low discount rates (timing). The number of IRRs is a different issue (unconventional flows).

questions.stem: Hartwell Foods must choose one of two mutually exclusive lines at R = 10%. Line S costs $35,000 and has an IRR of 28.57% and an NPV of $5,909.09. Line L costs $150,000 and has an IRR of 20.00% and an NPV of $13,636.36. What is the source of the conflict and the correct choice?
options: Scale: choose Line S, which has the higher IRR
Scale: choose Line L, which has the higher NPV
Timing: choose Line S, which pays back sooner
No conflict: accept both lines because both NPVs are positive
questions.explanation: Line L is more than four times as large, so its lower percentage return still earns more dollars. That is a scale conflict, and NPV settles it. Taking both is impossible because the lines are mutually exclusive, and choosing S by IRR is the mistake of picking the higher IRR.

questions.stem: For two mutually exclusive projects at R = 10%, Project A has an IRR of 28.03% and an NPV of $13,388.43, while Project B has an IRR of 22.98% and an NPV of $15,522.16. Which project should the firm take?
options: Project B, because it has the higher NPV
Project A, because it has the higher IRR
Both, because both have positive NPVs
Neither, because the two rules disagree
questions.explanation: When the rules conflict for mutually exclusive projects, the NPV rule decides, because NPV measures the dollars added to shareholder wealth. Project B adds more even though its IRR is lower.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a reason why the IRR and NPV rules can rank mutually exclusive projects differently?
options: The projects differ in the scale of the investment
The projects' cash flows arrive at different times
NPV uses cash flows while IRR uses accounting profit
IRR is a percentage that ignores how many dollars are invested
questions.explanation: Both NPV and IRR are built from the same cash flows, so the basis of the numbers is not the cause. Conflicts come from scale (IRR ignores dollars invested) and from timing (the NPV ranking changes with the discount rate, the IRR does not).

questions.stem: For independent projects with conventional cash flows, the NPV rule and the IRR rule always give the same accept or reject decision for each project.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: For conventional flows NPV is positive exactly when IRR exceeds R, so accept/reject decisions match. Disagreements arise only when projects are mutually exclusive and must be RANKED.

questions.stem: Two mutually exclusive projects, E and L, have IRRs of 20.50% and 17.72%. Their NPV profiles cross at 13.24%. At R = 10% the NPV of L is higher. If the firm's required return rises to 15%, what happens to the conflict?
options: It disappears: above the crossover rate E has both the higher IRR and the higher NPV
It gets worse, because L always has the higher NPV
It stays, because the IRR ranking and the NPV ranking never agree for these projects
It disappears because both projects now have negative NPVs
questions.explanation: Above the crossover rate (13.24%) the profile of E lies above that of L, so E wins on NPV as well as IRR and the two rules agree. At 15% both NPVs are still positive, because both IRRs exceed 15%.

questions.stem: Put these steps for choosing between two mutually exclusive projects in the right order. (a) Pick the project with the highest positive NPV. (b) Discount each project's cash flows at R to get its NPV. (c) Forecast each project's after-tax cash flows. (d) Decide on the required return R.
options: d, c, a, b
b, c, d, a
c, d, b, a
c, b, d, a
questions.explanation: The NPV sequence from the lecture is: cash flows, then the discount rate, then discount (equalising lives if needed), then decide. The IRR is not needed to make the final choice.

questions.stem: Why does the choice between the IRR rule and the NPV rule only matter for two mutually exclusive projects when R is BELOW the crossover rate?
options: Below the crossover both projects have negative NPVs, so neither rule applies
Below the crossover each project's IRR changes sign, so the IRRs are unreliable
Below it the lower-IRR project has the higher NPV; above it the two rankings agree
Above the crossover the projects become independent, so both can be taken
questions.explanation: At the crossover rate the two NPVs are equal. Below it the lower-IRR project (bigger or later flows) is ahead on NPV; above it the higher-IRR project is ahead on both measures. The rules therefore disagree only below the crossover.

questions.stem: Compare a project with cash flows concentrated in year 1 with a project of equal cost whose cash flows come mostly in year 5. When the required return rises, what happens to their NPVs?
options: The earlier-payoff project's NPV falls faster, because it is discounted first
The later-payoff project's NPV falls faster, so its NPV profile is steeper
Both NPVs fall at the same speed because they have the same cost
Both NPVs rise, because a higher R means a higher required return
questions.explanation: Cash flows far in the future are discounted by (1 + R)^t, so a higher t makes the present value more sensitive to R. That is why back-loaded projects win at low R and lose at high R, which creates the timing conflict.

questions.stem: The firm must pick exactly one of three mutually exclusive projects, each with a positive NPV at its required return. P1: IRR 31%, NPV $4.1 million. P2: IRR 22%, NPV $9.8 million. P3: IRR 16%, NPV $7.4 million. Which should it take?
options: P1, which has the highest IRR
P3, which has the lowest IRR and so the most room to grow
All three, since each NPV is positive
P2, which has the highest NPV
questions.explanation: With more than two mutually exclusive projects, compute the NPV of each and choose the highest (the lecture's rule). The highest IRR (P1) is the trap of picking the highest IRR; the three cannot all be undertaken because only one can be chosen.

questions.stem: Fraser Valley Berry Co. can take only one upgrade. Plan E costs $60,000 and returns $39,000, $31,000 and $11,000 in years 1 to 3 (IRR 20.50%). Plan L costs $60,000 and returns $5,000, $28,000 and $58,000 (IRR 17.72%). At R = 10% per annum, by how many dollars does the NPV of the plan the firm should choose exceed the NPV of the other plan?
solution: L has the higher NPV although E has the higher IRR. Advantage of L = $11,262.21 − $9,338.84 = $1,923.37.

errors.label: Reported the NPV of the higher-IRR plan (E) as the answer
errors.explain: E has the higher IRR, but the question asks for the NPV advantage of the plan with the higher NPV.

errors.label: Subtracted NPV(L) from NPV(E)
errors.explain: The advantage of the better plan is positive; reversing the subtraction gives a negative number.

errors.label: Compared undiscounted net gains (31,000 vs 21,000)
errors.explain: Net gains ignore timing; the later cash flows of L must be discounted before comparing.

questions.explanation: At R = 10% (below the 13.24% crossover) L has the higher NPV even though E has the higher IRR. The IRR rule would have cost shareholders the difference.

questions.stem: Hartwell Foods must choose one of two mutually exclusive lines at R = 10% per annum. Line S costs $35,000 and returns $45,000 in one year (IRR 28.57%). Line L costs $150,000 and returns $180,000 in one year (IRR 20.00%). How much shareholder wealth is lost, in NPV terms, if the firm chooses by IRR instead of by NPV?
solution: Choosing S by IRR gives up 13,636.36 − 5,909.09 = $7,727.27 of NPV.

errors.label: Reported the NPV of Line S (the IRR choice)
errors.explain: That is what the IRR rule delivers, not what it gives up.

errors.label: Subtracted NPV(L) from NPV(S)
errors.explain: The loss is how much more NPV L has, a positive number.

errors.label: Compared undiscounted gains (30,000 − 10,000)
errors.explain: The gains arrive in a year and must be discounted at 10% before comparing.

questions.explanation: This is a scale conflict: L is four times the size, so its lower percentage return earns more dollars. The NPV rule picks L.

questions.stem: Prairie Wind Farms Ltd. has two mutually exclusive turbine projects at R = 7% per annum. Project S costs $30,000 and returns $14,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years (IRR 18.91%). Project L costs $110,000 and returns $46,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years (IRR 12.26%). What is the NPV of the project that maximises shareholder wealth?
solution: Project L has the higher NPV (despite the lower IRR), so it is the choice and its NPV is the answer.

errors.label: Reported the NPV of Project S (higher IRR)
errors.explain: S has the higher IRR, but the shareholders gain more from L.

errors.label: Used a 4-year annuity factor for L
errors.explain: Three years of cash flows need an annuity factor with N = 3.

errors.label: Added the flows without discounting
errors.explain: The three payments must be discounted at 7%; 3 × 46,000 − 110,000 ignores the time value of money.

questions.explanation: Here R = 7% is below the crossover rate (9.70%), so the larger project L wins on NPV even though S has the higher IRR.

questions.stem: At R = 8% per annum, mutually exclusive Project A (−$50,000; +$38,000, +$25,000, +$8,000) has an IRR of 25.84%, and Project B (−$50,000; +$9,000, +$18,000, +$53,000) has an IRR of 20.65%. What is the NPV of the project the firm should undertake?
questions.explanation: NPV(B) = −50,000 + 9,000/1.08 + 18,000/1.08² + 53,000/1.08³ = $15,838.54; NPV(A) = $12,969.31. B is chosen by NPV, even though A has the higher IRR. $2,869.23 is only the NPV advantage, and $14,665.32 comes from treating CF0 as a period-1 flow.

questions.stem: A firm picks Line S (cost $35,000, one-year payoff $45,000) over Line L (cost $150,000, one-year payoff $180,000) because S has the higher IRR. If R = 10% per annum, how much NPV does the firm give up?
questions.explanation: NPV(L) − NPV(S) = 13,636.36 − 5,909.09 = $7,727.27. $13,636.36 is NPV(L) alone, $5,909.09 is the NPV of the project actually taken, and $20,000 compares undiscounted gains (30,000 − 10,000).

questions.stem: If two mutually exclusive projects have IRRs of 24% and 21%, choosing the 24% project always maximises shareholder wealth.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: IRR ignores scale and timing. The 21% project can have the higher NPV (when R is below the crossover rate, or when it is much larger), and NPV is the measure of shareholder wealth.

questions.stem: The crossover rate is the discount rate at which the _____ of two projects are equal.
options: IRRs
NPVs
profitability indexes
payback periods
questions.explanation: At the crossover rate the two NPV profiles intersect, so both projects have the same NPV. IRRs are where each profile cuts the horizontal axis, which is a different point.

questions.stem: How is the crossover rate between Project A and Project B found?
options: It is the simple average of the two projects' IRRs
It is the IRR of the larger project, which has the larger flows
It is the IRR of the year-by-year differences in their cash flows (A − B)
It is the discount rate at which each project's NPV equals zero
questions.explanation: Subtract one project's cash flows from the other's in every period, including CF0, and find the IRR of the differences. The NPV of that difference is NPV(A) − NPV(B), which is zero exactly when the two NPVs are equal.

questions.stem: Prairie Wind Farms Ltd. compares Project S (−$30,000; +$14,000 in each of years 1 to 3) with Project L (−$110,000; +$46,000 in each of years 1 to 3). Which cash-flow list is used to find their crossover rate?
questions.explanation: Subtract the projects' flows period by period, and keep the difference in CF0 (−110,000 − (−30,000) = −80,000). Leaving CF0 out or adding the flows are the classic setup mistakes. The IRR of L − S is 9.70% (see the NPV check: −80,000 + 32,000 × annuity factor(9.701026%, 3) = $0.00).

questions.stem: How does the crossover rate of two projects differ from the IRR of one of them?
options: An IRR sets one project's NPV to zero; the crossover sets the gap between two NPVs to zero
The IRR needs a required return to compute, but the crossover rate does not
The crossover rate is always larger than both projects' own IRRs
They are the same number whenever the projects are mutually exclusive
questions.explanation: IRR is where one NPV profile hits the horizontal axis. The crossover rate is where two profiles meet each other, which may happen at a positive NPV. For conventional projects with a ranking conflict, the crossover is typically below both IRRs.

questions.stem: Subtracting Project B's cash flows from Project A's, rather than A's from B's, gives a different crossover rate.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Reversing the subtraction multiplies every difference by −1, which flips the sign of the NPV of the difference but not the discount rate at which it is zero. The textbook solution says it is irrelevant which project is subtracted from the other.

questions.stem: Why is the IRR of the difference in cash flows equal to the discount rate at which two projects have equal NPVs?
options: NPV(A) − NPV(B) equals the NPV of the difference flows, which is zero at the IRR of those flows
NPV is linear in the discount rate, so the profiles must meet at the average of the IRRs
The IRR of any project always equals the rate where its NPV is the same as another project's
Subtracting the flows removes the time value of money
questions.explanation: NPV is additive: NPV(A) − NPV(B) = NPV(A − B). Setting that to zero means finding the IRR of the difference. NPV is not linear in R, so the average of the IRRs has no special meaning.

questions.stem: The NPV profiles of E and L cross at 13.24%. E has the higher IRR (20.50% against 17.72%). The firm's required return is 9%. Which project should it choose, and why?
options: E, because 9% is below the 13.24% crossover rate and E has the higher IRR
L, because 9% is below the 13.24% crossover rate and L has the higher NPV there
E, because 9% is below both IRRs
L, because its IRR is lower and lower IRRs are safer
questions.explanation: Below the crossover rate, the project with the later cash flows (L) has the higher NPV. Above it, E would win. IRR size does not decide the ranking. At 9%, NPV(L) − NPV(E) = $2,574.92.

questions.stem: Fraser Valley Berry Co.'s Plan E costs $60,000 and returns $39,000, $31,000 and $11,000 in years 1 to 3. Plan L costs $60,000 and returns $5,000, $28,000 and $58,000. The crossover rate is 13.24%. At R = 12% per annum, which is below the crossover, how many dollars larger is the NPV of the better plan than the NPV of the other plan?
solution: 12% is below the 13.24% crossover, so L has the higher NPV by $8,068.97 − $7,364.02 = $704.95.
(As R climbs to 13.24% this gap shrinks to $0; above it E leads.)

errors.label: Subtracted NPV(L) from NPV(E)
errors.explain: The better plan's advantage is a positive amount.

errors.label: Reported the NPV of E, the higher-IRR plan
errors.explain: The question asks for the gap between the two NPVs, not the NPV of the higher-IRR plan.

errors.label: Compared undiscounted net gains (31,000 vs 21,000)
errors.explain: Net gains ignore timing; the later flows of L must be discounted at 12% before comparing.

questions.explanation: The gap between the two NPVs is positive below the crossover and shrinks to zero at it, which is the same as saying NPV(L − E) rises to zero as R moves up to the crossover.

questions.stem: Hartwell Foods compares two mutually exclusive lines. Line S costs $35,000 and returns $45,000 in one year. Line L costs $150,000 and returns $180,000 in one year. Find the cash flows of the incremental project (L − S) and then the crossover rate. (Final answer: crossover rate, % per annum.)
solution: Check: NPV of the difference at 17.391304% = −115,000 + 135,000/1.17391304 = $0.00 (to the cent).
Below 17.39% the larger line L has the higher NPV; above it the smaller line S does.

errors.label: Reported the IRR of Line S (28.57%)
errors.explain: That is S's own IRR, not the rate where the two NPVs are equal.

errors.label: Averaged the two IRRs (28.57% and 20.00%)
errors.explain: NPV profiles do not cross at the average of the IRRs; the crossover is the IRR of the difference.

errors.label: Added the flows (L + S) instead of subtracting
errors.explain: Adding the flows gives the IRR of a combined project, not of the incremental one.

questions.explanation: The crossover rate is the IRR of the incremental flows. For a one-year pair of projects it reduces to incremental payoff over incremental outlay, minus one.

questions.stem: Okanagan Cider Works compares mutually exclusive Project A (−$50,000; +$38,000, +$25,000, +$8,000) with Project B (−$50,000; +$9,000, +$18,000, +$53,000). The incremental flows A − B are 0, +$29,000, +$7,000 and −$45,000 in years 0 to 3. What is the NPV of A − B at R = 11% per annum?
solution: A negative NPV for A − B means NPV(A) < NPV(B): at 11% (below the 13.08% crossover) B is the better project.

errors.label: Computed B − A instead of A − B
errors.explain: The question asks for A − B; reversing it flips the sign (although the decision is the same).

errors.label: Treated the year-0 difference as a period-1 flow
errors.explain: The first difference is at time 0 (here it is zero); every flow was pushed out a year in this error.

errors.label: Added the differences without discounting
errors.explain: At R = 11% each difference must be discounted before adding.

questions.explanation: NPV of the difference equals NPV(A) − NPV(B). Its sign tells you which project is better at that rate, and it crosses zero at the crossover rate.

questions.stem: Fraser Valley Berry Co. compares Plan E (−$60,000; +$39,000, +$31,000, +$11,000) with Plan L (−$60,000; +$5,000, +$28,000, +$58,000). The IRRs are 20.50% for E and 17.72% for L. What is the crossover rate?
questions.explanation: The incremental flows E − L are 0, +34,000, +3,000, −47,000, and their IRR is 13.2445%. Check: NPV of the difference at 13.244485% = $0.0000, i.e. zero to the cent. 20.50% and 17.72% are the projects' own IRRs, and 19.11% is the average of the two IRRs, which has no special meaning.

questions.stem: Okanagan Cider Works compares mutually exclusive Project A (−$50,000; +$38,000, +$25,000, +$8,000) with Project B (−$50,000; +$9,000, +$18,000, +$53,000). The IRRs are 25.84% for A and 20.65% for B. What is the crossover rate?
questions.explanation: The incremental flows A − B are 0, +29,000, +7,000, −45,000, and their IRR is 13.0825%. Check: NPV of the difference at 13.082548% = $0.0001, i.e. zero to the cent. The wrong answers are the IRR of A + B (22.63%, adding instead of subtracting), the average of the IRRs (23.25%), and A's own IRR (25.84%).

questions.stem: Prairie Wind Farms Ltd. compares Project S (−$30,000; +$14,000 in years 1 to 3; IRR 18.91%) with Project L (−$110,000; +$46,000 in years 1 to 3; IRR 12.26%). What is the crossover rate?
questions.explanation: The incremental flows L − S are −80,000, +32,000, +32,000, +32,000, an annuity whose IRR is 9.7010% (annuity factor 2.5). Check: NPV of the difference at 9.701026% = −$0.0004, i.e. zero to the cent. 15.58% is the average of the IRRs, 13.70% the IRR of L + S, and 12.26% L's own IRR.

questions.stem: Two conventional projects have NPV profiles that cross once at a positive rate. Project X has the higher NPV at low discount rates, and Project Y has the higher NPV at high discount rates. Which statement about their IRRs and cash-flow timing is typical?
options: X has the lower IRR and its cash flows come later or are larger overall
X has the higher IRR and its cash flows come sooner
X and Y must have the same IRR
X has the lower IRR because its cash flows are smaller overall
questions.explanation: Back-loaded or larger cash flows make a steeper NPV profile: the project is worth more at low R but loses value faster as R rises, so it ends up with the lower IRR. The project that wins at high R has the flatter profile and the higher IRR.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the crossover rate is NOT correct?
options: It is the IRR of the difference between the two projects' cash flows
It equals the average of the two projects' IRRs
At that discount rate the two projects have the same NPV
Below it and above it, the ranking of the two projects by NPV is reversed
questions.explanation: The crossover has to be found from the incremental cash flows; there is no shortcut through the two IRRs. The other three statements describe it correctly (for profiles that cross once).

questions.stem: The NPVs of two mutually exclusive projects (F and G) are computed at several rates. At 10%: F $9,339, G $11,262. At 12%: F $7,364, G $8,069. At 14%: F $5,489, G $5,079. At 16%: F $3,706, G $2,277. Between which two rates does the crossover lie?
options: Between 10% and 12%
Between 12% and 14%
Between 14% and 16%
Below 10%, because G leads at 10%
questions.explanation: The crossover is where the NPV gap changes sign. G is ahead at 10% and 12% (gaps +1,923 and +705) and F is ahead at 14% (gap −409), so the sign change, and therefore the crossover, lies between 12% and 14% (the exact rate is 13.24%).

questions.stem: For mutually exclusive Projects S and L, the IRR of the incremental flows (L − S) is 9.70%. Project L is larger. The firm's required return is 8%. What should the firm do?
options: Take S: the incremental IRR is below the IRRs of both projects
Take S: its own IRR is higher than the incremental IRR
Take both, because the incremental IRR is positive
Take L: the incremental IRR of 9.70% exceeds the required return of 8%
questions.explanation: The incremental project L − S earns 9.70% on the extra money invested in L. If that exceeds R, the extra investment is worthwhile and L is better; if R were above 9.70%, S would be better. Comparing the incremental IRR with the individual IRRs is not the test.

questions.stem: Project X costs $50,000 and returns $30,000 in each of years 1 and 2. Project Y also costs $50,000 and returns $25,000 in each of years 1 and 2. The firm must pick one. What can be said about a crossover rate?
options: There is none at a positive rate: X beats Y at every discount rate
The crossover is at the IRR of X because X has the larger flows
The crossover is the average of the two IRRs
The crossover is at 0% because the outlays are equal
questions.explanation: The incremental flows X − Y are 0, +5,000, +5,000: all non-negative, so they have no IRR. X dominates Y: it is better in every year and NPV(X) > NPV(Y) at every R, so there is no ranking conflict.

questions.stem: The profitability index (PI) is the present value of a project's cash _____ divided by the present value of its cash outflows.
options: profits
inflows
tax shields
dividends
questions.explanation: PI = PV of cash inflows / PV of cash outflows. It is also called the benefit/cost ratio, and for a conventional project the outflow is the initial investment.

questions.stem: Which expression is the professor's profitability index (the usual, 1-based definition)?
options: NPV ÷ initial outlay (value added per dollar)
Initial outlay ÷ PV of cash inflows (cost per dollar of benefit)
NPV ÷ PV of cash inflows (value added per dollar of benefit)
PV of cash inflows ÷ PV of cash outflows
questions.explanation: The lecture defines PI = PV of inflows / PV of outflows and shows PI = 1 + NPV/initial outlay. NPV/outlay is the 0-based alternative, which ranks projects the same way but equals PI − 1 (easily mixed up with the accept cut-off of 1).

questions.stem: A manager says Project Z 'returns $1.18 of present value for every dollar we invest in it'. Which decision measure is she quoting?
options: The internal rate of return
The net present value
The accounting rate of return
The profitability index (benefit/cost ratio)
questions.explanation: PI is the 'bang for the buck': present value of benefits per dollar of cost, 1.18 here, meaning NPV is about 18% of the outlay. IRR is a percentage rate, NPV is a dollar amount, and ARR uses accounting profit.

questions.stem: A project has a profitability index of 0.96 at the firm's required return. What does this say?
options: It returns 96% per year, so it should be accepted if the required return is below 96%
NPV is positive because the PI is positive
Each dollar invested returns only 96 cents of present value, so NPV is negative and the project should be rejected
The project breaks even in present-value terms and the firm is indifferent
questions.explanation: PI < 1 means PV of inflows is less than PV of outflows, so NPV < 0 and the project destroys value. A PI of 0.96 is not a rate of return, and a PI is always positive even when NPV is negative. Indifference occurs at PI = 1.

questions.stem: At a required return of 9% per annum a conventional project has a profitability index of exactly 1.00. What are its NPV and IRR?
options: NPV = $0 and IRR = 0%
NPV = $0 and IRR = 9%
NPV = 1 and IRR = 9%
NPV is negative and IRR is above 9%
questions.explanation: PI = 1 means PV of inflows equals the outlay, so NPV = 0. NPV is zero exactly when the discount rate equals the IRR, so the IRR is 9%.

questions.stem: A project has an initial outlay of $120,000 and the present value of its later cash inflows is $132,000. What are its profitability index and NPV?
questions.explanation: PI = PV of inflows / outlay = 132,000/120,000 = 1.10, and NPV = 132,000 − 120,000 = $12,000. 0.10 is the 0-based figure (NPV/outlay), 0.91 inverts the ratio (120/132), and $132,000 is the PV of inflows, not the NPV.

questions.stem: How do the 1-based PI (PV inflows ÷ PV outflows) and the 0-based version (NPV ÷ initial outlay) compare?
options: The 0-based figure is the 1-based figure minus 1; they rank projects identically but have different accept cut-offs (1 and 0)
They give the same numbers, because both are called the profitability index
The 0-based figure is always larger, so it accepts more projects
They rank projects differently, so a firm must pick one definition and stay with it
questions.explanation: The lecture warns there are two definitions and that adding or subtracting one gives the same rankings. The trap is comparing a 0-based figure with the cut-off of 1: a 0-based 0.12 is a good project, not a reject.

questions.stem: Why does the PI rule always give the same accept or reject decision as the NPV rule for a conventional project?
options: Because PI uses the project's IRR as its discount rate, so the two rules always agree
PI > 1 exactly when PV of inflows exceeds the outlay, which is exactly when NPV > 0
Because PI is simply the NPV expressed as a percentage of the PV of inflows
Because both rules ignore the size of the project
questions.explanation: NPV = PV of inflows − outlay, and PI = PV of inflows / outlay. NPV is positive when the PV exceeds the outlay, and PI is above 1 under exactly the same condition. They differ only in how they RANK projects.

questions.stem: A conventional project (a single outlay at time 0, inflows afterwards) with a profitability index of 1.15 has an NPV equal to 15% of its initial outlay.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: PI = 1 + NPV/outlay, so NPV = outlay × (PI − 1) = 0.15 × outlay. For example, an outlay of $60,000 gives an NPV of $9,000.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT true of the profitability index?
options: It is also called the benefit/cost ratio
A value above 1 means the project has a positive NPV (conventional flows)
It measures the value created per dollar invested
It is expressed in dollars, so it shows how much wealth the project creates
questions.explanation: PI is a ratio, so it says nothing about the dollar size of the NPV. That is why it can rank mutually exclusive projects badly. The other statements are standard.

questions.stem: Kootenay Brewing's project costs $26,000 and returns $11,500, $12,400 and $9,800 in years 1 to 3. Its PI is 1.16 at a required return of 6%, 1.04 at 12% and 0.99 at 15%. At which of these required returns should the firm accept it?
options: At 15% only
At all three rates
At 6% only, because it has the highest PI there
At 6% and 12% only
questions.explanation: Accept when PI > 1. The PI falls as R rises and crosses 1 at the IRR (14.57%), so the project is acceptable at 6% and 12% but not at 15%. Accepting at 6% only treats the highest PI as the only acceptable one.

questions.stem: Kootenay Brewing's project costs $26,000 now and returns $11,500, $12,400 and $9,800 at the end of years 1, 2 and 3. The required return is 9% per annum. What is the profitability index? (Two decimals.)

errors.label: Reported the 0-based index NPV ÷ outlay
errors.explain: That is PI − 1. The usual PI divides the PV of inflows by the outlay and is compared with 1.

errors.label: Divided the outlay by the PV of inflows
errors.explain: PI puts the benefits on top: PV of inflows over outlay.

errors.label: Used undiscounted inflows
errors.explain: The inflows are in years 1 to 3 and must be discounted at 9% first.

questions.explanation: PI is PV of inflows divided by the outlay. Enter the inflows with CF0 = 0 so that the calculator's NPV is a pure present value, then divide.

questions.stem: Muskoka Marine plans a boatyard. It spends $80,000 now and a further $35,000 at the end of year 1. Cash inflows of $60,000, $65,000 and $70,000 follow at the end of years 2, 3 and 4. The required return is 10% per annum. Using PI = PV of inflows ÷ PV of outflows, what is the PI? (Two decimals.)

errors.label: Counted only the $80,000 initial outlay as the outflow
errors.explain: The year-1 spending is also a cost; the PV of ALL outflows goes in the denominator.

errors.label: Subtracted the PV of the year-1 spending from the inflows
errors.explain: Netting the later cost against the inflows changes the ratio. The lecture definition keeps inflows on top and ALL outflows below.

errors.label: Reported PI − 1
errors.explain: That is the 0-based figure, NPV ÷ PV of outflows.

questions.explanation: With a second outlay after time 0, the denominator is the PV of all outflows. Discount the year-1 cost one period; the inflows start in year 2 and are discounted two to four periods.

questions.stem: A project has an initial outlay of $84,000 and an NPV of $17,640 at the firm's required return. What is its profitability index? (Two decimals.)
solution: PI = PV of inflows / outlay = (outlay + NPV)/outlay = 1 + NPV/outlay

errors.label: Reported NPV ÷ outlay (0.21)
errors.explain: That is the 0-based index. Add 1 to get the usual PI.

errors.label: Divided the NPV by the PV of inflows
errors.explain: PV of inflows is outlay + NPV = $101,640, and PI puts it on top of the outlay, not under the NPV.

errors.label: Divided the outlay by the PV of inflows
errors.explain: The ratio is the other way round: benefits over costs.

questions.explanation: Since NPV = PV of inflows − outlay, PV of inflows = outlay + NPV and PI = 1 + NPV/outlay.

questions.stem: Okanagan Cider Works is considering a project that costs $28,000 and returns $9,000, $10,500, $8,200 and $6,000 at the end of years 1 to 4. The required return is 16% per annum. What is the profitability index? (Two decimals.)

errors.label: Reported the 0-based index PI − 1
errors.explain: That is negative here, and the cut-off for the usual PI is 1.

errors.label: Used undiscounted inflows
